items.description: Businessman Farooq Oreagba, popularly known as Mr. Steeze, has reflected on the highs and lows of his financial journey, revealing that he went from being a dollar millionaire at the age of 30 to working as a labourer in England just five years later after losing his banking job. Oreagba made the revelation during an appearance on Ebuka Obi-Uchendu’s MENtality show, co-hosted by Banky W, where he spoke about wealth, materialism and the importance of life over money. During the conversation, Oreagba posed a hypothetical question to Ebuka to illustrate his belief that life is more valuable than any amount of wealth. “Ebuka I’m going to drop a few nuggets here. How much is money to you. Will a billionaire dollar satisfy you?” he asked. Responding, Ebuka said, “I’m not looking for satisfaction.” Oreagba continued, “Okay now I’m going back to the first question about materialism and people chasing money but if I gave you 10 million dollars now, what would you say?” Ebuka replied, “What would I say? I’ll call you from Miami to thank you.” Oreagba then added, “But what if I told you you can have it but not live more than 24 hours to spend it what would you do?” Ebuka responded, “I mean I could make 10 million dollars, so it’s not worth it.” Using the exchange to make his point, Oreagba reflected on his own experience with wealth and hardship. “Right. Then all of a sudden living now has more value. I was a dollar millionaire at 30, at 35 I was working as a labourer in England. I had my dream and all them I lost my job as a banker. To maintain that lifestyle I was hustling, doing all kinds of stuff… I had my priorities wrong. Sometimes we place priorities on….” Oreagba said the experience taught him that many people spend too much time chasing money while neglecting what truly matters, noting that wealth alone does not define the value of life. items.title: Ablakwa meets Jamaican Foreign Minister ahead of Mahama’s historic state visit
items.description: Ghana’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, has met with his Jamaican Foreign Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith, in Kingston, Jamaica, ahead of President John Dramani Mahama’s historic state visit to the Caribbean nation. The meeting formed part of preparations for President Mahama’s visit, which is being undertaken at the invitation of Jamaican Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness. During the engagement, the two Foreign Ministers expressed optimism about the prospects of deepening cooperation between Ghana and Jamaica and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations in areas including trade, culture, maritime affairs, education, health, and other sectors of mutual interest. Welcoming Minister Ablakwa to Kingston, Senator Kamina Johnson Smith described it as a pleasure and honour to receive Ghana’s Foreign Affairs Minister, particularly during Jamaica’s emancipation and independence celebrations. “It is an absolute pleasure and honour to welcome you once more to Kingston, Jamaica, and how much more pleasure it gives us that this is your visit during our emancipation and independence celebration time,” she said. She said the Jamaican government was looking forward to receiving President Mahama, adding that his visit in response to Prime Minister Holness’ invitation was a source of pride for the country. “The government of Jamaica not only welcomes you, but looks forward very much to welcoming your president tomorrow evening, President John Dramani Mahama,” Senator Johnson Smith said. Minister Ablakwa thanked the Jamaican government for the warm reception and said Ghana was honoured to accept the invitation extended by Prime Minister Holness. “It’s always a pleasure to be here. And I want to thank you and the team for the very warm reception since our arrival. We are here to honour the invitation of Prime Minister Andrew Holness,” he said. He said Ghana was looking forward to President Mahama’s visit, describing it as a historic engagement that would be impactful and meaningful. “We are really looking forward to the arrival of President John Dramani Mahama on this historic visit. We promise this to be very impactful, very meaningful,” Ablakwa added. Senator Johnson Smith outlined activities planned for the state visit, including President Mahama’s address to a joint sitting of Jamaica’s Parliament, which she described as one of the highlights of state visits. “Among the things which are being anticipated will include the President’s address to the Parliament. This address to the joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament is something which is a pinnacle of our state visits,” she said. She also announced that President Mahama would lay a wreath at the shrine of Jamaica’s first national hero, the Right Honourable Marcus Garvey, whom she noted had influence on Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah. The programme will also include a visit to Seville, a heritage site where Ghana’s delegation will learn about Jamaica’s African heritage and the history of the transatlantic slave trade. Senator Johnson Smith said the visit would also provide an opportunity to continue discussions on the reparations agenda, noting President Mahama’s role in pushing the issue at the United Nations General Assembly. The Jamaican Foreign Minister added that President Mahama would be formally welcomed with a full military guard at King’s House and would participate in cultural activities, including a visit to a major cultural event and a reparations dialogue at the University of the West Indies. Minister Ablakwa expressed appreciation for what he described as a carefully planned programme and said President Mahama was excited about the visit. “He is very honoured that you have the opportunity to be the first Ghanaian president to address your joint sitting of Parliament,” Ablakwa said. He added that the President would also hold bilateral engagements with Prime Minister Holness, the leader of the opposition, and other stakeholders. The Foreign Affairs Minister further disclosed that President Mahama would endorse Jamaica’s petition on the reparations agenda, reaffirming Ghana’s support for the shared pursuit of justice. “He would also be endorsing Jamaica’s petition,” Ablakwa said. Both ministers described Ghana and Jamaica as partners united by shared history and common interests, pledging to continue working together to strengthen relations between the two countries. “We are still collaborators, working together in the struggle. Our way to justice is achieved,” Senator Johnson Smith said. Minister Ablakwa added: “We are really, really excited that in Jamaica we have our own family. We are on the same page, in the same struggle.”

items.title: How many African countries will qualify for Women’s World Cup through WAFCON?
items.description: The 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) in Morocco will not only crown the continent’s champions but also determine which African teams will book their places at the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil. With Africa’s allocation increased for the expanded Women’s World Cup, the continent has a chance to send up to six teams to the global tournament. How many African teams will qualify? A total of four African countries will qualify automatically for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup. These will be the four semifinalists at the 2026 WAFCON. Once a team reaches the semi-finals, it secures a direct ticket to Brazil. In addition, two more African nations will have another opportunity to reach the World Cup by competing in the FIFA inter-confederation play-offs. This means Africa could ultimately have as many as six representatives at the 2027 Women’s World Cup if both play-off teams successfully qualify. How qualification works The 2026 WAFCON features 16 teams, divided into four groups of four. The qualification process is as follows: Four groups of four teams each. The top two teams in every group advance to the quarter-finals. The four quarter-final winners progress to the semi-finals. Those four semi-finalists qualify automatically for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup. The two losing quarter-finalists with the best overall tournament performance will earn places in the FIFA Women’s World Cup play-offs. WAFCON 2026 tournament details Host: Morocco Dates: July 26 – August 16, 2026 Teams: 16 Groups: Four groups of four teams Automatic World Cup qualification spots: Four Inter-confederation play-off spots: Two Africa’s possible representatives at Brazil 2027 Depending on the results, Africa will have: 4 teams guaranteed at the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup. Up to 6 teams if both play-off representatives secure qualification. items.title: AMA passes out metro guards, warns against corruption
items.description: The Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) has passed out 20 newly trained Metro Guards, with Mayor of Accra, Michael Kpakpo Allotey, delivering a strong warning against corruption, extortion, absenteeism, abuse of authority and other forms of misconduct that could undermine public confidence in the Assembly. According to a post shared on Facebook he recruits, who constitute the 14th batch of AMA Metro Guards, officially completed their training during a passing-out ceremony held at the Assembly’s Head Office on Thursday, July 30. The ceremony, held under the theme “Service, Discipline and Commitment to the People within the Accra Metropolis,” marked the Assembly’s first passing-out parade for newly recruited Metro Guards since 2016, signaling renewed efforts to strengthen the city’s enforcement capacity. Addressing the graduating recruits, Mayor Michael Kpakpo Allotey expressed satisfaction with the addition of the new officers to the Assembly’s enforcement workforce but stressed that the true measure of their success would depend on how they conducted themselves in the field. He noted that the extensive training the recruits had undergone would count for little if they failed to uphold the discipline, professionalism and ethical standards expected of officers entrusted with maintaining order within the capital. According to the Mayor, the training and passing-out ceremony would be meaningless if the recruits allowed themselves to engage in acts that eroded public trust in the Assembly. He urged the officers to carry themselves with dignity and to treat members of the public with respect, emphasizing that their daily conduct would shape public perception not only of the Metro Guards but of the entire Accra Metropolitan Assembly. “The way you conduct yourselves will determine how residents perceive both you and the Assembly,” he stressed, reminding the recruits that professionalism, fairness and integrity must remain the foundation of their service. The Mayor emphasised that no officer would receive special treatment should they engage in illegal or unethical conduct. He warned that any recruit who violated the law would face the full consequences of their actions, irrespective of the fact that they had only recently completed training or were employees of the Assembly. The warning comes amid growing public calls for greater accountability among city enforcement personnel, who often serve as the first point of contact between the Assembly and residents during enforcement exercises. Mayor Allotey also challenged the recruits to resist pressure from within the system. He encouraged them to report any superior officer who directed them to engage in unlawful, corrupt or unethical practices, assuring them that his office would stand firmly behind officers who acted with integrity. The Mayor pledged that officers who demonstrated honesty, professionalism and commitment to the Assembly’s values would receive recognition and opportunities for advancement. He explained that promotions and other incentives under his administration would be based on merit rather than favouritism. According to him, hard work, integrity and actions that enhanced the Assembly’s image and improved service delivery would form the basis for career progression. Beyond corruption, Mayor Allotey expressed concern over what he described as negative attitudes exhibited by some existing officers. He cautioned the new recruits against adopting poor work habits, particularly absenteeism and neglect of duty. The Mayor specifically criticized instances where some officers reportedly abandoned their assigned posts and returned home to sleep during working hours instead of carrying out their responsibilities. He urged the graduates to distinguish themselves through discipline, commitment and dedication to duty. Mayor Allotey explained the significance of the Metro Guards’ distinctive black-and-white uniform. According to him, the colours represent the diverse situations, personalities and challenges officers would encounter while performing their duties across the metropolis. He reminded the recruits that although the uniform carries symbolic meaning, its true value depends on the conduct of those who wear it. The Mayor therefore urged the officers to ensure that the uniform was never “stained” by corruption, extortion, indiscipline or any other form of misconduct capable of tarnishing the Assembly’s reputation. The Metropolitan Coordinating Director of the Accra Metropolitan Assembly, Mr. Douglas Annoful, administered the oath of allegiance to the graduating officers during the ceremony. As part of the oath, the recruits pledged to faithfully serve the Assembly, uphold professionalism and maintain the integrity of the institution throughout their careers. They further committed themselves to refraining from collecting unauthorized monies or fees from members of the public while performing their official duties—a practice that has often generated complaints against some enforcement personnel in the past. The oath also underscored the Assembly’s renewed commitment to promoting transparency, accountability and ethical conduct among its enforcement staff. The ceremony also celebrated excellence among the graduating officers, with three recruits receiving awards for exceptional performance during the training programme. Edward Kotey Ashie was honoured as Best in Drill, having demonstrated exceptional precision, discipline and command during parade exercises. Patience Ahiekpor received the Best in Academics award for emerging as the top performer in the theoretical component of the training programme. Augustine Appiah was recognised as the Most Disciplined Recruit, an award reflecting exemplary conduct, commitment and adherence to the standards expected throughout the training period. The 20 recruits who successfully completed the programme and received certificates were: Patrick Quaye, Emmanuel Apenteng, Eric Asiedu, Zillah Amarteifio, Evans Yamoah, Isaac Amoah, Bright Ahiable, Theophilus Kpakpo Allotey, Irene Owoo, Daniel Tagoe, Martin Adotey, Stephen Quartey, Mavis Sackey, Robert Kornor, Isaac Appiah Koduah, Augustine Appiah, Patience Ahiekpor, Emmanuel Odonkor, Ismaila Quaye and Edward Kotey Ashie. The passing-out ceremony marks a significant milestone for the Accra Metropolitan Assembly, representing the first graduation of newly recruited Metro Guards in ten years. The recruitment and training of the 14th batch is expected to strengthen the Assembly’s capacity to enforce city by-laws, maintain public order and support ongoing efforts to improve sanitation, decongest streets and promote discipline across the capital. With a renewed emphasis on integrity, professionalism and accountability, the Assembly hopes the new officers will contribute to restoring public confidence in municipal enforcement while advancing its broader vision of building a cleaner, safer and more orderly Accra.

items.title: Certification ISO 9001 : ce qu’elle prouve et ce qu’elle ne prouve pas [Par Aboubacar Sakho]
items.description: La certification ISO 9001 est aujourd'hui l'une des références internationales les plus reconnues en matière de management de la qualité. Adoptée par des entreprises, des administrations publiques et des organisations à travers le monde, elle atteste qu'une structure applique un système de management conforme à des exigences internationalement reconnues. Pour les partenaires, les investisseurs et les usagers, elle constitue un gage de sérieux et d'engagement dans une démarche d'amélioration continue. En revanche, elle ne doit pas être assimilée à une garantie de performance globale. Élaborée par l'Organisation internationale de normalisation (ISO), la norme repose sur plusieurs principes essentiels : l'orientation client, le leadership, l'implication du personnel, l'approche processus, la prise de décision fondée sur des données et l'amélioration continue. Son objectif est d'aider les organisations à mieux structurer leur fonctionnement, à maîtriser leurs activités et à améliorer durablement leurs résultats. L'obtention de cette certification est conditionnée par un audit réalisé par un organisme indépendant, chargé de vérifier que les processus sont correctement définis, appliqués et évalués. Des audits de suivi sont ensuite effectués afin de s'assurer que les exigences de la norme continuent d'être respectées. Cette démarche présente de nombreux avantages. Elle améliore l'organisation interne, renforce la maîtrise des processus, réduit les risques d'erreurs, favorise la traçabilité des activités et consolide la confiance des partenaires. Dans certains secteurs, elle représente également un avantage concurrentiel et peut constituer une condition d'accès à certains marchés. Pour autant, l'ISO 9001 ne garantit ni la rentabilité d'une entreprise, ni son efficacité opérationnelle, ni l'absence de dysfonctionnements. Elle ne certifie pas non plus la qualité d'un produit ou d'un service en particulier et ne signifie pas qu'une organisation est la meilleure de son secteur. Même certifiée, une entreprise peut être confrontée à des difficultés financières, à des retards ou à des réclamations de ses clients. À l'inverse, une entreprise peut afficher d'excellentes performances sans disposer de cette certification. Son succès dépend avant tout de la pertinence de sa stratégie, de la qualité de son management, des compétences de ses collaborateurs, de sa capacité d'innovation, de sa maîtrise des coûts et de sa faculté à répondre aux attentes de ses clients. De nombreuses entreprises, notamment des PME mais aussi certaines grandes sociétés, appliquent des méthodes de gestion efficaces sans rechercher la certification ISO 9001. Elles peuvent choisir de ne pas s'engager dans cette démarche en raison de son coût, des contraintes qu'elle implique ou simplement parce que leur marché ne l'exige pas. Cela ne les empêche pas d'être performantes, rentables et reconnues pour la qualité de leurs prestations. La principale différence réside dans la reconnaissance externe. Une organisation certifiée bénéficie d'une validation officielle délivrée par un organisme indépendant, attestant que son système de management répond aux exigences de la norme. Une organisation non certifiée peut atteindre le même niveau d'organisation, mais sans cette reconnaissance formelle. L'ISO 9001 doit être considérée comme un outil d'amélioration et de gouvernance plutôt que comme une finalité. Elle traduit la volonté d'une organisation de structurer ses pratiques selon des standards internationaux et d'inscrire son fonctionnement dans une logique de progrès permanent. Toutefois, la véritable performance repose avant tout sur la qualité du leadership, la compétence des équipes, la pertinence des choix stratégiques et la capacité à produire des résultats concrets. Une entreprise performante n'est donc pas nécessairement certifiée ISO 9001, tout comme une entreprise certifiée n'est pas automatiquement performante. La certification constitue un atout et un signe de maturité organisationnelle, mais elle ne remplace ni la vision, ni l'innovation, ni l'efficacité managériale, qui demeurent les véritables moteurs de la réussite. Par Aboubacar SAKHO Expert en communication L’article Certification ISO 9001 : ce qu'elle prouve et ce qu'elle ne prouve pas [Par Aboubacar Sakho] est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Is Gen Z Really Saving Hollywood?
items.description: Sometime after Jack Black hollered “chicken jockey” in 2025’s A Minecraft Movie , and before The Odyssey drove the masses mad with aspect-ratio anxiety, Hollywood finally felt seen—and saved—by Gen Z. Over the past year, trade publications and mainstream outlets alike celebrated the news: Zoomers were coming of age and coming to the rescue of American cinema. Their theater attendance purportedly outstripped that of their elders; their tastes in video-game franchises and low-budget horror undeniably carried the day. These cheery headlines largely traced back to a single report by Fandango conducted in January. In a survey of 7,000 adults in the United States, the Gen Z responses were eye-popping: 87 percent had watched at least one film in theaters in the previous 12 months; the average Zoomer had seen seven movies in that period. Compare this with Gen X at 70 percent and 6.1 movies, respectively. (It should be noted, though, that Fandango’s survey pool drew disproportionately from movie enthusiasts: 5,091 of the respondents had gone out to see at least one film in the previous year.) It might seem predictable that Gen Z now drives the box office. The youngest Zoomers are entering high school (and thus making their first independent purchases), and the eldest are rounding out their 20s (and thus reaching for the next rungs on the career ladder). Many of them are in the season of life when discretionary income rises to meet peak discretionary time. But the seemingly outsize fanfare around these numbers makes more sense in light of the turmoil of the past few years. After the upheaval of the coronavirus pandemic, followed by the writers’ and actors’ strikes that snarled the production pipeline, many industry observers feared that Zoomers were a lost demographic. This cohort of young adults, historically a core part of Hollywood’s customer base, had come of age at a moment when there were fewer new things to watch and more reasons—such as streaming—to stay inside. [ Read: The fear of missing The Odyssey ] Theatrical films “don’t have a future if you can’t capture the younger audiences of today, who are going to be the older audiences of tomorrow,” Paul Dergarabedian, a senior analyst for Rentrak, a box-office-research firm, told me. Fandango’s study, which was released ahead of CinemaCon, the annual convention of theater owners, told the industry what it wanted to hear: that people would continue going to the movies. But the big picture is murkier. “I think that there’s a lot to be optimistic about, but I would not put the return of theatrical back at the feet of Gen Z,” Kevin Goetz, the CEO and founder of Screen Engine, a research and analytics firm, told me. “I wouldn’t proclaim victory quite yet.” Although other surveys also observe strong youth turnout, the proportions are far less dramatic. Pew, for example, found in a survey last summer that 67 percent of people ages 18 to 29 had seen a movie in the theater in the past 12 months. This year brought real evidence of cinema’s appeal to the youth: The runaway success of Backrooms and Obsession marked the coronation of YouTube auteurs as bankable directors and drew notably fresh-faced crowds. Even with such turnout, this year’s box office is unlikely to return to the heights it regularly reached in the past. More people are staying at home: In 2019, the share of the non-moviegoing population was 24 percent, according to Vista Group, which provides analytics and software for the film industry; in 2024, that number hit 30 percent. People who still go to the cinema do so less often: In 2025, theaters in the U.S. and Canada sold approximately two tickets per capita, less than half of what they sold in 2002. Other surveys, from more disinterested sources than Fandango, indicate that although theater attendance has somewhat recovered from its pandemic lows, Gen Z sees fewer movies than past generations of youth. In fact, the drop-off is starkest among young people: In 2007, according to data provided to me by Gallup, 18-to-29-year-olds went out to see an average of nine films. In 2025, the same demographic saw 4.3 movies. As their moviegoing frequency has fallen, Gen Zers’ habits have started to converge with those of the general moviegoing population, Matthew Liebmann, Vista Group’s chief product, innovation, and marketing officer, told me. In other words: Kids today don’t behave that differently from older people. The numbers point to a broader behavioral shift. Moviegoing used to be a matter of habit meeting spontaneity. Teens loitering at the mall, couples on a date, friends gathering for a night out—these groups reliably showed up at the multiplex and would pick a showtime once they were already in the door. Today, patrons generally plan their cinema visits in advance, and the question of what to see has collapsed into the question of whether to go at all. Once moviegoing went from routine hangout to major outing, theaters had to adapt. Many have, over time, diversified their offerings. In a phone call, Bob Bagby, the CEO of B&B Theatres, rattled off a cruise line’s worth of activities now offered at his various locations, including mah-jongg, trivia, and bingo. Some locations have bocce and pickleball courts; other chains have added ropes courses and axe-throwing. “I’ve seen it,” Bagby told me, of the latter. “Our insurance people said No, no, don’t do that .” [ Read: The great Gen Z dividing line ] But even the core elements of the cinema experience have changed. If you’re going to get people to look up from the screen in their palm, you have to offer the biggest one possible. If seating is reserved, it needs to be sumptuous. (One theater-chain president told me that its recliners had heating and cooling settings.) If there’s going to be dining, you might consider rolling out a multicourse prix fixe menu —or at least an array of hot options. If your lobby is being treated like a special destination, it should also look the part. “The Gen Z crowd wants to come in and be somewhere cool,” says Penn Ketchum, the managing partner of the theater chain Penn Cinema, describing the 24-tap self-serve beer wall he installed in one location as part of a $2 million renovation. “They don’t want to come through a dingy, dusty, aged lobby. They want to come in from the parking lot and be somewhere that’s worthy of being in the background of their picture.” Over time, “people have been trained to spend more at the theater when they go,” Alicia Reese, a senior vice president of equity research for media and entertainment at the financial firm Wedbush Securities, told me. This is a boon for theaters, because concessions have much higher margins than the films themselves. Moviegoing now comes with an air of occasion. In an era of screen abundance, Hollywood has tried to differentiate the theatrical release by creating an artificial sense of scarcity and transience. The industry has borrowed the tactics of touring artists and fashion drops , promoting limited premium-format screenings and slinging special-edition popcorn buckets. But encouraging audiences to associate moviegoing with “all the trimmings and treats,” Liebmann said, also has drawbacks: It creates an “affordability misperception,” which may dampen their appetite for regular visits. Gen Z may be filing into more auditoriums than expected these days. And even if they’re doing so less often than their predecessors, and even if their seats are bigger and squishier and spaced less densely than before, their presence certainly ensures some kind of future for the theatrical model. But when you consider the experience that’s been retooled around them, one that depends on so many things beyond sitting in a dark room together as a projector rattles, it’s hard to shake the sense that the pictures have gotten small.

items.title: Let Them Eat Gold
items.description: W hen you approach the freshly gilded twin statues near the Lincoln Memorial, there is no mistaking that they are gold. Very, very gold. Distractingly gold—or, more precisely, covered in 23.75-karat gold leaf costing $5.1 million. The 19-foot statues, called The Arts of War , were once easy to miss but now look a bit like oversized children’s trophies, especially next to the classical and austere Lincoln Memorial. Seeing them is as if, on the walk between Arlington National Cemetery and the National Mall, you’d suddenly stumbled upon a P. F. Chang’s. This is how President Trump is approaching his redecoration of Washington: glitzy and gaudy, even if out of place. He has already splashed gold all around the White House, but these statues are the most prominent symbols of Washington’s new gilded age. As the scaffolding around the statues came down this week, marking one of the few completions of a Trump-ordered renovation project, the president giddily posted photos on social media—and tourists, commuters, cyclists, and runners paused to take photos of their own of the capital’s latest can-you-believe-it attraction. Trump has worn his love of gold like a blinging billboard. Mar-a-Lago’s ballroom is inspired by Versailles, and he has proudly bragged of golden bathrooms, golden airplane-seatbelt buckles, and a gold-infused penthouse suite. The Oval Office now looks like a Middle Eastern bazaar crossed with an opulent Cracker Barrel. Thick, gold frames line the walls; gold vases and ice buckets adorn the fireplace mantle; gold stars form a circle on the ceiling; and gold appliqués fill any gaps. (Trump insists that these are real gold, and not painted flourishes from Home Depot.) Last year, he exempted gold bullion from his reciprocal tariffs , and he named his special visa program for wealthy foreigners the Trump Gold Card . He has taken his personally designed presidential challenge coin (which is golden) and glued it to the center of the Oval Office door, at about eye level. The coasters are gold, the curtains are gold, and guests know to come bearing gifts of gold. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ( left ) and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles sit in the Oval Office on February 2. (Alex Wong / Getty) When FIFA President Gianni Infantino awarded Trump the first FIFA Peace Prize , it was a golden orb of a trophy. Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook presented the president with a 24-karat-gold base to hold a glass sculpture. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last year gave him a golden pager to commemorate an operation in which members of Hezbollah were killed when their pagers detonated. “See,” he said during a meeting with his Cabinet in March while riffing about all of the projects he’d launched in Washington, “I’m a gold person.” It’s one thing for Trump to have a personal fascination with one of the world’s most expensive metals. It’s another for the president to flaunt it at a time when many Americans are struggling to pay rent, losing their health insurance, and seeing high prices at the gas pump. It may not quite be a “Let them eat cake” moment, but it is one where he seems to be saying: Let them see that I just spent $5 million in taxpayer funds on golden statues. T rump for decades has loved gold and marble, liberally sprinkling them about his development projects and his personal spaces. Ivana Trump, his first wife, who was the Trump Organization’s vice president of interior design, encouraged Trump’s gold obsession, according to Regime Change , the recent book by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan that has a golden cover. (Ivana’s love of the color proved lasting: She was buried in a gold casket.) In the 1980s, Trump bought Mar-a-Lago in South Florida and went on to put $7 million worth of gold leaf on the walls, plus gold-plated sinks near the ballroom. He hired the designer Henry Conversano, known for infusing golden flourishes in the Golden Nugget casinos, to remodel his Trump Tower penthouse apartment and work at his Atlantic City casino. In 1988, he purchased from the sultan of Brunei a yacht that was bathed in gold—couches, sinks, ceilings—and named it the Trump Princess. [ Read: A decade of golden-escalator politics ] “It was so gaudy. Almost shockingly gaudy. And he loved it. He thought it was the most beautiful thing out there,” Jack O’Donnell, one of Trump’s former casino executives who helped him host parties on the boat, told me. He speculated that Trump may have been inspired by the yacht when he remade the Lincoln Bathroom almost entirely in gold and marble. Years later, in 2008, when Trump built a hotel in Las Vegas, the 406,000-square-foot facade was coated in a layer of gold-infused glass. More recently, when a group of Trump supporters erected a 22-foot statue of him at his golf course in Doral, Florida, they opted for a gold finish. “To him gold was the essence of richness and class,” Barbara Res, who oversaw construction for the Trump Organization and was placed in charge of building Trump Tower, told me. “To him it meant, This is gold. This is mine. It’s the best you can get, and I’m the best. That’s how his mind works. I’m going to show you the best by buying the best. ” Sometimes, she said, it wasn’t the best. It was a cheaper alternative that looked like gold but actually wasn’t (although she found that he was willing to spend his money for something that was his idea). He liked the design concept trompe l’oeil , a French word that means “deceive the eye,” where painters could make a column that looked like marble. “It was tricking the eye of the consumer. He loved it,” Res said. “And he took an interest in the gold finishes. It reflects his taste and his ability to spend endless money on something beautiful. That’s what he wants people to believe.” Whether it’s in his long, red ties; his swooshed-over hairstyle; or his “Thank you for your attention to this matter” social-media posts, Trump is all about branding. Perhaps nothing is more on-brand for him than his affection for gold. “I love the gold, but if you don’t use 24 karat gold, it doesn’t look good,” he told reporters last August. “It just beams,” he marveled in September. “It’s all real stuff,” he said in March. “You can’t imitate it. Someday they’ll discover a paint that will look like gold, and the guy’s going to be the richest man in the world.” Peter York, a design and culture columnist, wrote in Politico Magazine in 2017 that Trump’s design style is “aspirational, meant to project the wealth so many citizens can only dream of.” Although it’s often associated with Italian Renaissance or French Baroque, York says a better comparison is more recent. “The best aesthetic descriptor of Trump’s look, I’d argue, is dictator style,” he wrote. [ Read: The YOLO presidency ] Gold has often been used to represent imperial power, whether in 18th-century France or 19th-century Russia. When Trump went to the Middle East for his first foreign trip of his second term, I watched as he marveled at the gold and marble in the palaces of Doha and Abu Dhabi. “Versailles is not a gold leaf,” he said in June ahead of a trip to the palace. “Versailles is the real deal.” President Trump receives a tour of the Chateau de Versailles from French President Emmanuel Macron on June 17. (Anna Moneymaker / Pool / AFP / Getty) T he two Arts of War statues , called Valor and Sacrifice , were sculpted by Leo Friedlander and cast in Italy. They were dedicated in 1951, offered to the United States as a gift from the Italians for helping rebuild their country after World War II. Each statue shows a nude man and a seminude woman. Two other statues, collectively called The Arts of Peace , are nearby but still undergoing their golden glam-ups. Each of the statues sits on a granite pedestal ringed with 36 stars, representing the states in the Union at the end of the Civil War. The statues, cast in bronze, were last regilded in 1971 and had since faded. Trump added them to the list of eyesores he wanted fixed before the nation’s 250th birthday, on July 4, and federal officials scrambled to meet his demands. [ Read: ‘Rush project at request of POTUS’ ] When I reached out to the White House to ask about the project, the president’s role in it, and his choice of gold, the spokesperson Davis Ingle responded with a statement that made no mention of gold and said, in part: “No other president has done more to beautify our Nation’s interior than President Trump.” He said that the president’s “bold vision” was ensuring that the 250th birthday was filled with “glory and pride.” He referred other questions to the Department of Interior, which did not address any of my questions about the project, its delays, the choice to heavily apply gold, or Trump’s involvement. “Residents and visitors are excited to see the city revitalized to the grand destination it was meant to be,” the department offered in a statement. Federal officials did not seek competitive bids for the work on the statues, bypassing the typical process and awarding a contract in April for $5.1 million. The project was treated as a high priority by the National Park Service, according to The New York Times , which cited internal documents that referred to it as “a visible, high-impact example of how the N.P.S. is responding to presidential directives.” Extensive market research was not done to determine whether $5 million was a fair price, according to documents obtained by NOTUS , and the agency determined that only one company could meet the requirements of the work and the timeline: the Gilders’ Studio in Maryland. The company, which did not respond to my message, has done a large number of regilding projects around the country, including the dome of the Georgia State House, the cupola of Faneuil Hall in Boston, and—perhaps most similar to the statues in Washington—the Sherman Monument in Central Park. A description of the project had a mandatory competition date of July 1. But for the past few weeks, as it had for the months before, the scaffolding remained up, and tarps read: We are making DC safe and beautiful. Only now is the project coming into view, and although Trump is clearly pleased, others are less so. “Fit for an oligarch’s ballroom,” a review in ARTNews reads. As I rode my bike past the new gilded statues Friday morning, I couldn’t help but wonder what would next succumb to Trump’s Midas touch. If a triumphal arch is constructed across the bridge, will it be just as glaringly golden? Will Trump cast the John F. Kennedy statue outside the Kennedy Center in gold? Is Abraham Lincoln, sitting nearby, at risk? Or the pensive Thomas Jefferson standing in the dome across the way? How far will Trump’s new golden age extend?

items.title: Which Screen Is the ‘Good Screen’ Now?
items.description: The videos that Instagram suggests in my never-ending “For You” feed are usually of a constellation of women. They’re strangers, but I call them “my girls.” One of them is remodeling her house; one is always cleaning and “resetting” the van she lives in; one is sampling pasta and sandwiches at various New York establishments. And each has something special that I can’t explain to you—a je ne sais quoi, a curious style of speaking—so I’ve come to look forward to my regular glimpses of their lives, which I get when I scroll in bed before I go to sleep each night. I regard these strangers as my intimates in a way, even though some of them are not people I think I would like if I actually met them. One morning, I was watching one on my living-room television while sipping my coffee. My husband walked into the room and winced as one of the women changed into a perfect re-creation of an American Girl–doll outfit (very theater kid, not his thing). I felt a flash of defensiveness—she makes everything by hand! She has a real sense of self! Not to mention a seemingly sweet relationship with her father and pet birds. I kept scrolling and was relieved that another one of my girls hadn’t appeared. She often records herself eating a frozen dinner on her couch while watching police body-cam footage on YouTube to unwind. And I mean no disrespect to her, but if she had shown up, I would have lunged for the remote. You might be wondering: Why was I watching Instagram on my TV? Instagram’s vice president of product, Tessa Lyons-Laing, has referred to TV as the company’s “ next frontier .” As it tries to compete with YouTube and Netflix, Instagram is apparently looking for ways to be … both of them. And so it has launched a stand-alone service for various streaming devices, which it recently expanded with new features to help “friends and family watch together.” This caught my attention: I wanted to try taking the “bad” screen (my phone) and putting it onto the “good” screen (my TV) to see how it would make me (and the people around me) feel. [ Read: The flip-phone cleanse ] Years ago, the “good screen versus bad screen” meme originated as a joke about having an office job. The “bad” screen was a desktop computer at work, whereas the “good” screen was a personal laptop, full of one’s own, delightful, self-chosen digital activities. But in 2022, following the coronavirus-pandemic lockdowns, the writer Kate Lindsay noted a shift . When people referred to the “bad” screen, they now seemed to be talking about their smartphone, which they felt hopelessly dependent on, and when they mentioned the “good” screen, they were referring to the humble television, which now felt wholesome and safe. “We’re so convinced that it’s in our best interest to reverse the effects of social media that even watching a 30-minute TV show uninterrupted seems constructive,” Lindsay observed. But maybe, four years later, the 30-minute-show part is negotiable. Perhaps “good” could come just from giving our thumbs a break, looking up instead of down, and permitting other people to see what we’re doing. My husband was initially wary of adding his Instagram account to our living-room TV, but he acquiesced, and we had kind of a blast watching his feed together. Most of the videos were of male comedians I didn’t recognize; I sounded like the trope of a Boomer mom as I repeatedly asked, “Do you know him?” whenever a new guy showed up. I didn’t mean “Are you friends?”; I meant “Are they Your Guys?” Sometimes they were, and I was honored to meet them. Sometimes they weren’t; they were just guys. We both laughed to the point of tears at a video that some guy had shared of his dad trying to teach him to bunt a baseball when he was 10 years old. I manually liked it with the remote control and then sent it to myself, from my husband, via direct message. On my TV. “This intrigues me,” Jonathan Gray, a professor of media and cultural studies at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, told me when I asked him about the app. Scrolling has always had a social element, he said, and people will often show a funny or interesting video to the person next to them. But he was skeptical of whether they would want to share every bit of their feed with their loved ones. “It’s one thing when I turn my phone to my wife and say, ‘Hey, you’ll like this,’ but 90 percent of what I see, she won’t want to watch,” he said. “It seems kind of painful.” Plus, his wife is learning how to whittle at the moment, and he doesn’t want to watch a bunch of whittling videos. [ Read: The extras are tired ] Gray also noted that the recommendation algorithms sometimes take big swings and throw new things at users to learn whether they’ll be interested. One might worry a little about the big swings that could appear on your TV, which to others in the room might appear to be something you’ve already expressed enthusiasm about. When I asked the Instagram spokesperson Christine Pai whether the TV app would filter out any weird stuff, she told me that both apps are using the same recommendation system. (The only specific difference she cited is that the TV app will give an edge to horizontal videos, because they are better suited for the display.) The app does allow users to play themed “channels” based on their preestablished interests, so you don’t necessarily have to show off your entire, highly variable and sometimes unpredictable feed. The idea with the channels seems to be that making the secret, private shame of scrolling into a collaborative activity will give it a new place in the home. It can be more like watching America’s Funniest Home Videos together after dinner and less like sitting side by side, staring silently at something in your lap. People feel ambivalent about scrolling feeds, Marika Lüders, a professor of media and communication at the University of Oslo, wrote to me on this point. We find it entertaining at times, but we also feel embarrassed and guilty about it. To her, moving Instagram from a phone to a TV seems like “a strategy to increase the status of short-form videos,” by putting them on a screen that people (currently) feel less anxiety about. That makes sense to me, though I find it just as easy to imagine how this may backfire for the company. Many people who are attempting to cut back on their Instagram use remove the app from their phone and use only the desktop-computer version, which is clunkier and less comfortable to scroll through for hours. Using it is so nonintuitive and unnatural that it calls attention to the absurdity of one’s habit. Moving Instagram to a bigger screen, then, is usually a route not to normalizing it in that new space but instead to severing ties with it altogether. The differences between a phone and a TV are even more dramatic and may be even more off-putting. Surely the novelty will wear off. Last week, while visiting my sister-in-law and her boyfriend, my husband and I asked them to show us their feeds on their TV. My sister-in-law’s was funny because it was full of wedding-planning content—she’s currently waiting on the requisite engagement ring—and because she kept getting videos of this one baby who’s obsessed with Bad Bunny. Her boyfriend got a hairless cat, a guy pretending to be Wolverine, and a recipe for butter-chicken macaroni and cheese. Those were a little funny, too, but because you don’t know him, you don’t get why and you don’t care. After 20 minutes or so, we got bored of the experiment and left for a baseball game. Later, in the quiet of my hotel room, I went back to my own, private phone.

items.title: SSGC assures citizens there is no gas leak, says odourisation plant testing led to complaints
items.description: The Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) said on Sunday that complaints of a suspected gas leak near Karachi’s Abul Hasan Isphahani Road since the previous night were due to the testing of odourisation plants during the commissioning of a new pipeline. While gas is often thought to have a distinctive smell, it is in fact odourless. Gas suppliers deliberately add odorants to the gas as a safety measure to alert consumers to potentially life-threatening leaks. In a media alert issued on Sunday, the SSGC said that odourants used to give gas its distinctive smell were added in larger quantities for testing purposes. This resulted in a stronger-than-usual smell, prompting reports of a gas leak from various parts of Karachi. “The SSGC administration wishes to make it clear that all system pressures are normal and that no gas leak of any kind has been reported,” the statement said. “The smell is solely due to the relatively larger quantity of odourants added to the gas during the testing of the odourisation plants.” The company requested its customers to remain calm and continue their regular activities. Gas leaks can be life-threatening, causing explosions and fires as well as death by suffocation. In January, three women suffocated to death, while another fainted in a gas leak incident in an apartment in Rawalpindi’s Bahria Town Phase VII.

items.title: La Tunisie enregistre 220 décès par noyade chaque année
items.description: Malgré les efforts déployés pour renforcer le dispositif de sauvetage, les noyades demeurent un défi majeur pour la sécurité publique en Tunisie, qui compte 1 300 kilomètres de côtes et des centaines de plages propices à la baignade notamment lors de la saison estivale. Selon les données officielles, les plages tunisiennes ont enregistré 31 décès par noyade au cours de la saison de baignade 2025 (de juin à octobre), contre 34 lors de la saison 2024. Parallèlement, les unités de la Protection civile ont mené des milliers d’opérations de sauvetage ; au pic de la saison, en août, le rythme des interventions a atteint environ 24 opérations par heure, incluant des cas de noyade ainsi que divers autres incidents en mer. Les statistiques nationales — compilées depuis 2020 sous la supervision du ministère de la Santé et avec la participation de diverses parties prenantes — indiquent que la Tunisie enregistre en moyenne environ 220 décès par noyade chaque année ; ces incidents surviennent en mer, dans des barrages, des puits, des piscines, des canaux d’irrigation et divers autres plans d’eau. Dans ce contexte, le Dr Mohamed Ridha Arrab, chef de la sous-direction des urgences médicales et de la médecine de catastrophe à l’Office national de la protection civile, a déclaré aux médias que les unités de la protection civile avaient réussi à sauver 454 personnes de la noyade au cours de la dernière saison, tout en enregistrant environ 90 décès dans leur périmètre d’intervention. Il a toutefois précisé que ces chiffres diffèrent des statistiques nationales globales, qui regroupent des données provenant de sources variées. L’article La Tunisie enregistre 220 décès par noyade chaque année est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Top 10 countries paying highest minimum wages in 2026
items.description: Minimum wage policies differ widely around the world, with some countries guaranteeing workers more than three times what others pay for the same number of hours. While higher wages are often linked to a country’s cost of living, productivity and labour laws, they also reflect efforts to ensure workers can maintain a decent standard of living. Several high-income economies continued to raise their wage floors in 2026 to keep pace with inflation and labour market pressures, with European nations dominating the rankings. Below are the 10 countries offering the highest statutory minimum wages in 2026, based on official national rates. U.S. dollar conversions are approximate and based on exchange rates in early 2026. 1. Luxembourg Luxembourg continues to top the global rankings with the highest statutory minimum wage. The country adjusts its wage floor in line with inflation and conducts formal reviews every two years. Workers with recognised qualifications earn more than the standard minimum. 2026 minimum wage Skilled workers (18+): €3,244.48 per month (about $3,792 ) Unskilled workers (18+): €2,703.74 per month (about $3,160 ) 2. Australia Australia remains among the world’s best-paying countries for minimum wage earners. The national rate is reviewed every year by the Fair Work Commission, while employers are also required to make compulsory superannuation contributions on behalf of workers. 2026 minimum wage A$24.95 per hour (about US$16.87 ) Equivalent to roughly US$2,830 per month for full-time employment 3. Ireland Strong economic growth and regular wage adjustments have helped Ireland maintain one of Europe’s highest minimum wages. The country ranks among the leading employers in terms of statutory pay. 2026 minimum wage €2,391 per month (about US$2,794 ) 4. Germany Germany continues to strengthen worker protections through regular increases to its national minimum wage. The latest adjustment benefits millions of employees, with another rise already planned for 2027. 2026 minimum wage €13.90 per hour (about US$16.24 ) 5. Netherlands The Netherlands updates its minimum wage twice each year, allowing workers’ earnings to reflect changing economic conditions. Holiday allowances also provide additional income beyond regular wages. 2026 minimum wage €14.71 per hour (about US$17.19 ) 6. Belgium Belgium combines a national minimum wage with sector-specific agreements that often guarantee even higher pay. The country’s wage system is supported by strong collective bargaining. 2026 minimum wage €2,154.11 per month (about US$2,517 ) 7. United Kingdom The UK’s National Living Wage increased again in 2026 as part of the government’s commitment to maintaining wages at around two-thirds of median earnings for eligible workers. 2026 minimum wage £12.71 per hour (about US$16.82 ) 8. New Zealand New Zealand reviews its minimum wage annually, with the rate applying to most workers aged 16 and above. The country remains one of the highest-paying labour markets in the Asia-Pacific region. 2026 minimum wage NZ$23.50 per hour (about US$13.38 ) Approximately US$2,335 per month for full-time workers 9. France France’s minimum wage, widely known as the SMIC, is automatically adjusted to account for inflation and broader wage trends, helping preserve workers’ purchasing power. 2026 minimum wage €1,823.03 per month (about US$2,130 ) 10. Canada Canada rounds out the top 10, although it does not operate a single nationwide minimum wage. Instead, each province and territory sets its own rate, resulting in significant differences across the country. 2026 minimum wage C$15.00 to C$19.75 per hour , depending on the province (about US$10.84 to US$14.28 per hour) Vanguard News The post Top 10 countries paying highest minimum wages in 2026 appeared first on Vanguard News .

6 soldiers killed, 75 residents abducted as bandits attack Zamfara community
items.description: By Idris Salisu, Gusau At least six military were reported to have been killed by the suspected bandits abducting over seventy (70) residents of Kasuwar Daji in Kaura-Namoda local government area of Zamfara state. Sources from the area told Vanguard via telephone that, the suspected bandits attacked Kasuwar Daji community around 11:30 pm Saturday night after over running the military outpost station in Kasuwar Daji. The sources who confirmed the incident, alleged that 6 Soldiers were killed and over 70 people were abducted to the bush attacking several number of shops to loot properties. A resident who identified himself as Alhaji Aminu Kasuwar Daji, told our correspondent that the bandits who stormed the community in large numbers, immediately started shooting sporadically to overrun the military outpost based to protect the area. “Our calls to Zamfara state and the Federal Government is to come to the aide of Zamfara people generally on this insecurity bedivelling the state. We really in danger as if the bandits can overpowered military and succeeded in their operation on innocent citizens,” Aminu Kasuwar Daji said. While speaking to Vanguard through telephone interview, the former deputy speaker Hon Namadi Kasuwar Daji, said the bandits confirmed attacked his community and abducted unspecified number of residents. According to him, even though he was not around as he travelled out of the state, but his relatives called and told him about the bandits attacked which became a horrible situation. ” I was told that the bandits have even killed soldiers but I was not told the actual number, again I was told that the bandits after looting shops to do away with foodstuffs, drinks and other properties, have also abducted unspecified number of residents to the bush. Contacting the Police Public Relations Officer of the state Command DSP Yazid Abubakar, said he was not aware of the attacked at Kasuwar Daji, but promised to call back after contacting the head of Police Officer at the area. The PPRO could not respond to the several calls did to him to get back on the promised made as at the time of filing this report. The post 6 soldiers killed, 75 residents abducted as bandits attack Zamfara community appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: KNUST calls for collective action to tackle student mental health, financial pressures
items.description: The Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Kumasi (KNUST) has called for a collective approach to addressing growing challenges facing students, including mental health concerns, financial pressures, loneliness and career uncertainty, saying student well-being is a shared responsibility essential to producing resilient and socially responsible graduates. The call was made during the second edition of the Directorate of Student Affairs (DoSA) Day, held on the theme, “Promoting a Collective Stakeholder Commitment to Student Affairs.” Speaking at the event, KNUST Pro Vice-Chancellor, Professor David Asamoah, said universities must go beyond academic instruction to create environments that enable students to thrive intentionally. He noted that while academic excellence remains central to the University’s mission, producing ethically grounded, emotionally resilient and socially responsible graduates is equally important. “It reminds us that student affairs is everyone’s responsibility. A great university is not measured solely by its infrastructure, research output or global rankings, but by the quality of graduates it produces,” he said. According to him, today’s students face unprecedented challenges, including mental health concerns, financial pressures, loneliness, career uncertainty and the distractions of an increasingly digital world. Professor Asamoah urged students to make use of the support systems available through the Directorate of Student Affairs. “Seek help whenever you need it. Do not suffer in silence. Participate actively in leadership programmes, student organisations, volunteer activities and mentorship opportunities,” he advised. Director of Student Affairs, Professor Marian Asantewah Nkansah, said the Directorate exists to support students throughout their university journey to ensure they enjoy a fulfilling and rewarding campus experience. “Our goal is to help students become not just graduates, but well-rounded personalities who will carry our institution’s name forward and contribute meaningfully to nation building,” she said. She explained that DoSA Day was introduced to highlight the Directorate’s interventions and deepen appreciation of its role in promoting students’ welfare. “The DoSA Day initiative was instituted to showcase to the entire university community, especially to our students and stakeholders, the initiatives and interventions that we have put in place for our students’ well-being,” Professor Nkansah said. Chairman of the DoSA Day Planning Committee, Professor Samuel Asamoah Sakyi, described the celebration as an opportunity to strengthen collaboration among stakeholders while recognising excellence in student support. He encouraged participants to actively engage in the day’s activities, build partnerships and familiarise themselves with the range of support services available to students. “Student affairs is not the responsibility of one directorate alone, but the shared responsibility of the entire university community and its stakeholders,” he said. As part of the celebration, the Directorate honoured 40 former and current staff members for their outstanding contributions to student affairs at KNUST. The awardees included former directors, deans, vice deans, administrative heads, hall masters, senior tutors and other staff whose dedication has helped shape student life and welfare at the University.

items.title: NDLEA Intercepts China, Italy-bound cocaine shipment concealed mortar, backpack
items.description: By: Kingsley Omonobi Operatives of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) have intercepted consignments of cocaine concealed in local mortar and the false bottom of a backpack, packaged for shipment to China and Italy, respectively, through a logistics company in Lagos. According to the agency, the seizures were made by NDLEA officers of the Directorate of Operations and General Investigations (DOGI) on Thursday, 30th July 2026. They include 250grams of cocaine, factory fitted into the base of a local mortar packed in a carton for export to China, and 500grams of the same Class A drug hidden in the false bottom of a backpack being shipped to Italy. NDLEA also disclosed that its operatives in Rivers State arrested a 38-year-old notorious drug dealer, Ugo Gift Okonkwo, at Eagle Island Port Harcourt, following credible intelligence. The agency said the suspect was nabbed with various quantities of cannabis, cocaine, methamphetamine, swinol, tramadol and codeine syrup at the time of his arrest on Sunday, 26th July. Additionally, NDLEA officers on a stop-and-search operation at DMGS roundabout, Onitsha, Anambra State on Monday, 27th July intercepted a truck marked XK 131 BDG loaded with 26,000 bottles of codeine syrup weighing 3,960kg while the truck driver, Chinedu Nwanze, 40, was arrested. It said another 33, 1.84 kilograms of skunk were recovered from a Toyota Sienna bus with registration number KUJ 26 DV along Kwale/Ughelli expressway, Delta State on Sunday, 26th July, In Nasarawa State, NDLEA officers on Tuesday, 28th July arrested a 64-year-old man, Joseph Nwaeke, with 68kg of skunk and 29grams of methamphetamine at Asso Angwan Muazu, Karu area of the state. In Zamfara, NDLEA operatives on patrol along Zaria- Gusau highway on Monday, 27th July intercepted a suspect, Sani Umar, 27, conveying 7,400 pills of tramadol 225mg suspected to be supplies for criminal elements. With the same vigour, Commands and formations of the Agency across the country continued their War Against Drug Abuse (WADA) sensitization activities to schools, worship centres, workplaces and communities among others in the past week. These include: WADA enlightenment lecture to students and staff of Hausawa Special Primary School, Kano; Royal Crown School, Oluyole, Ibadan; Government Secondary School, Ibi, Taraba; and drivers at Challenge Bus Terminal Park, Ibadan, Oyo State, among others. Chairman/Chief Executive Officer of NDLEA, Brig. Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (rtd) commended the officers and men of DOGI, Rivers, Anambra, Delta, Nasarawa, and Zamfara Commands for the various successful operations, He enjoined them and their colleagues across the country to continue with the ongoing balanced approach to the drug control efforts of the Agency. The post NDLEA Intercepts China, Italy-bound cocaine shipment concealed mortar, backpack appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Après la crise migratoire à Sebta, les experts mettent en garde contre un risque de nouvelles vagues
items.description: Quelques jours après la tentative de passage massif vers les enclaves de Sebta et Melilla occupées, qui a vu des dizaines de milliers de jeunes, de femmes et de mineurs tenter de rejoindre le territoire espagnol, la question d'une éventuelle répétition de tels événements se pose avec acuité. Pour plusieurs chercheurs marocains, les conditions ayant conduit à cette crise demeurent largement présentes, laissant craindre de nouvelles tentatives à l'avenir. Le bilan humain reste particulièrement lourd. Selon les estimations relayées par plusieurs sources, plus d'une centaine de personnes seraient mortes ou portées disparues au large de Sebta, dont un grand nombre n'ont toujours pas été identifiées. Cette tragédie relance le débat sur la gestion de la migration irrégulière, aussi bien par l'Espagne que par l'Union européenne. Dans l'immédiat, Rabat et Madrid se sont accordés sur le retour des personnes ayant rejoint Sebta à la nage au cours des derniers jours. Cette décision vise à apaiser les tensions provoquées par un afflux que les autorités espagnoles elles-mêmes disent ne pas avoir anticipé. La gestion de cette crise a par ailleurs suscité de nombreuses réactions critiques au sein de la communauté internationale. Pour Mohamed El Khachani, spécialiste des questions migratoires, les événements de Sebta pourraient se reproduire si les causes profondes ne sont pas traitées. Selon lui, les seules mesures sécuritaires ne suffisent pas à empêcher ce type de mouvements de population. Le chercheur estime que les motivations des candidats à l'exil dépassent largement la seule question du chômage. Si le manque d'opportunités reste un facteur important, il souligne que beaucoup de jeunes nourrissent avant tout l'espoir de trouver de meilleures conditions de vie en Europe, parfois en idéalisant les perspectives offertes de l'autre côté de la Méditerranée. Mohamed El Khachani considère également que la question migratoire est intimement liée à des enjeux géopolitiques plus larges. Il rappelle que le Maroc ne peut être considéré comme le « gardien des frontières » de l'Espagne ou de l'Union européenne. Le chercheur évoque également les difficultés économiques et sociales ainsi que la lutte contre la corruption comme des éléments qui alimentent le sentiment de frustration chez une partie de la population. De son côté, Khalid Chayat, professeur de relations internationales à l'Université Mohammed Premier d'Oujda, estime que le débat doit dépasser la seule dimension migratoire. Selon lui, la présence des enclaves de Sebta et Melilla constitue un élément central de la problématique et mérite, à ses yeux, une discussion politique plus approfondie entre Rabat et Madrid. L'universitaire appelle ainsi à un dialogue fondé sur davantage de transparence et de confiance entre les deux pays afin de prévenir une instrumentalisation politique ou géopolitique de ces territoires. Il estime qu'une relation bilatérale stable entre le Maroc et l'Espagne est indispensable pour réduire les tensions récurrentes autour des questions migratoires. Au-delà des analyses divergentes sur les causes profondes de la crise, les spécialistes s'accordent sur un point : tant que les facteurs économiques, sociaux, politiques et géopolitiques resteront présents, le risque de nouvelles tentatives de migration irrégulière vers Sebta et Melilla demeurera élevé. Les récents événements rappellent ainsi que la réponse à cette problématique ne peut reposer uniquement sur des dispositifs de contrôle aux frontières, mais nécessite également une approche globale et durable. The post Après la crise migratoire à Sebta, les experts mettent en garde contre un risque de nouvelles vagues appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Daaray Kaamil, le sanctuaire du savoir et de l’héritage de Serigne Touba
items.description: Au cœur de la ville sainte, entre la Grande Mosquée et le cimetière de Touba, se dresse un haut lieu de conservation du savoir et de la mémoire : la bibliothèque « Daaray Kaamil » (« La Maison du Coran »). Véritable écrin du patrimoine intellectuel mouride, cet espace abrite une partie importante de l’héritage laissé par Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba, à travers ses écrits, des exemplaires du Saint Coran, des archives et une documentation riche destinée aux chercheurs, aux disciples et aux visiteurs. Dès l’entrée de la salle de lecture, le visiteur est plongé dans l’univers spirituel du fondateur du mouridisme. Une pensée de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba, affichée en plusieurs langues, rappelle la place centrale du savoir et de la spiritualité : « Mon trésor est le Saint Coran, la tradition du Prophète et les règles de bonne conduite, nullement l’accumulation d’argent ou d’or. » Une autre recommandation invite les chercheurs à la persévérance dans l’apprentissage : « Toi qui veux acquérir le savoir, révise à chaque fois, à chaque instant. » Ces enseignements trouvent une traduction concrète dans l’activité quotidienne de la bibliothèque. Des élèves de daara, des enseignants, des chercheurs et des fidèles y viennent pour approfondir leurs connaissances et mieux découvrir l’œuvre de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. Assis devant un ouvrage qu’il recopie soigneusement, Mbaye Guèye, pensionnaire d’un daara situé à Thiarène, dans la commune de Keur Madiabel (département de Nioro du Rip), profite de la période du Grand Magal pour fréquenter la bibliothèque. « Je viens ici à la quête du savoir et pour mieux connaître Serigne Touba, mon guide religieux », explique-t-il. À ses côtés, Cheikh Niang, professeur de philosophie au lycée de Sédhiou, consacre une partie de ses vacances à l’étude des écrits religieux. Comme lui, de nombreux visiteurs fréquentent « Daaray Kaamil » pour explorer l’immense production littéraire de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. Devant les rayonnages consacrés aux xasaïd, l’étonnement est souvent au rendez-vous. « C’est énorme ! », s’exclame Sokhna Asta Guèye, impressionnée par l’ampleur de cette collection. Selon Ousseynou Diattara, agent de la médiathèque, la bibliothèque accueille également de nombreuses délégations diplomatiques de passage à Touba, désireuses de découvrir ce patrimoine. L'oeuvre de Serigne Abdoul Ahad Mbacké La bibliothèque « Daaray Kaamil » est l’une des grandes réalisations de Serigne Abdoul Ahad Mbacké, troisième Khalife général des mourides. Construite en 1977 durant son khalifat (1968-1988), elle est composée de plusieurs espaces organisés autour de son mausolée. Le bâtiment abrite notamment une salle d’exposition retraçant son histoire, une médiathèque moderne équipée d’un espace de lecture, d’un studio de télévision numérique et d’écrans diffusant des xasaïd. Une autre salle est entièrement dédiée à l’œuvre littéraire de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. Ses écrits y sont classés méthodiquement par thèmes sur plusieurs rayonnages. D’autres espaces conservent des exemplaires du Saint Coran, des effets personnels du fondateur du mouridisme, ainsi que des archives administratives et historiques. « Daaray Kaamil » apparaît aujourd’hui comme un lieu de transmission où se perpétue l’héritage intellectuel et spirituel de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. Un sanctuaire du savoir qui fait dialoguer mémoire, recherche et foi au cœur de Touba. Salla GUEYE

items.title: Fonds souverain : des économistes invitent la Guinée à éviter le « syndrome hollandais »
items.description: La question de la création d'un fonds souverain en Guinée continue d'alimenter les réflexions du monde économique. Le 1er août 2026, le deuxième vice-gouverneur de la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG), Dr Almamy 2 Sylla, a insisté sur la nécessité de bâtir cet instrument financier avec méthode, patience et rigueur. Il s'exprimait à l'occasion de la deuxième conférence académique consacrée à la structuration optimale d'un fonds souverain en République de Guinée, organisée à l'Institut supérieur de commerce et d'administration des entreprises de Guinée (ISCAE). La rencontre a réuni des étudiants, des journalistes ainsi que plusieurs spécialistes des questions économiques autour d'un enjeu devenu central : la gestion des revenus issus de l'exploitation à grande échelle des ressources minières, en particulier celles du projet Simandou. Dans sa communication, Dr Almamy 2 Sylla a mis en garde contre toute précipitation dans la mise en place d'un fonds souverain. Selon lui, un tel mécanisme ne peut être efficace que s'il repose sur des excédents financiers durables. « Pour faire de notre République un paradis, la solution ne réside pas dans la précipitation, mais dans une construction graduelle, lente et sûre, en utilisant de façon optimale cet outil de souveraineté », a-t-il déclaré, avant de rappeler que la création d'un fonds souverain vise également à prémunir le pays contre le « syndrome hollandais », phénomène économique qui affecte certains pays riches en ressources naturelles lorsque les revenus issus des exportations déséquilibrent le reste de l'économie. Selon lui, la première condition reste l'existence de ressources pérennes. « On ne crée pas un fonds souverain sans générer, année après année, des excédents durables de devises. Si ces ressources sont temporaires ou insuffisantes, il n'y a aucun intérêt à mettre en place une telle structure », a-t-il expliqué. Dr Sylla a précisé qu'un fonds souverain constitue avant tout un cadre de gouvernance financière conforme aux meilleures pratiques internationales, permettant de gérer les excédents accumulés sur plusieurs exercices budgétaires plutôt que de les laisser improductifs. Il a également souligné qu'un fonds souverain représente un puissant levier financier susceptible de servir de garantie auprès des investisseurs, à l'image de ce que pratiquent plusieurs pays du Golfe. « Lorsque les recettes issues du pétrole, du gaz ou des ressources minières génèrent des excédents de devises, il est indispensable de les structurer efficacement afin de financer les grands projets de développement du pays », a-t-il insisté. Un mécanisme pour stabiliser l'économie et préparer l'avenir Invité à cette conférence, l'économiste Mohamed Camara, consultant associé gérant du cabinet Mokam Consulting, a rappelé que le fonds souverain constitue avant tout une épargne stratégique de l'État. Selon lui, ce mécanisme permet de faire face aux fluctuations des prix des matières premières. « Lorsque les prix de la bauxite ou du minerai de fer baissent, le fonds souverain permet de lisser les effets sur le budget de l'État », a-t-il expliqué. L'économiste a également insisté sur la dimension intergénérationnelle de cet outil : « Le fer et la bauxite sont des ressources non renouvelables. Si nous consommons toutes ces richesses aujourd'hui, que restera-t-il aux générations futures ? » Il estime également que le fonds souverain pourra faciliter le financement des infrastructures et servir de garantie pour mobiliser des ressources complémentaires auprès des partenaires financiers. Mohamed Camara a par ailleurs indiqué que les travaux de structuration du futur fonds sont déjà engagés par un cabinet mandaté par les autorités, tout en précisant que celui-ci devra être aligné sur les 24 principes de Santiago, les normes internationales de gouvernance applicables aux fonds souverains. Il a enfin appelé les universitaires, les chercheurs et les professionnels à enrichir les réflexions afin que le futur mécanisme réponde aux réalités spécifiques de la Guinée. Préparer les Guinéens au boom économique Administrateur général de Guineematin.com, Nouhou Baldé a estimé que cette réflexion dépasse le simple cadre technique. Pour lui, les Guinéens doivent être préparés aux transformations économiques susceptibles d'accompagner l'exploitation du projet Simandou. Il a rappelé que plusieurs pays riches en ressources naturelles n'ont pas réussi à transformer durablement leur boom économique en amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. Prenant l'exemple de l'Angola, il a évoqué la forte prospérité enregistrée au début des années 2010, avant de souligner la dépréciation du kwanza (la monnaie locale) et les difficultés économiques qui ont suivi. Selon lui, la Guinée doit tirer les leçons de ces expériences afin que les futures recettes minières profitent effectivement à la population. « Chacun doit devenir un acteur économique, que ce soit comme entrepreneur, citoyen ou décideur, afin de mieux tirer profit du boom économique attendu », a-t-il recommandé. Simandou, un levier potentiel pour un futur fonds souverain Présent également à la conférence, Cabinet Fofana, analyste politique et responsable de l'institut de sondage “Les Sondeurs”, estime que les perspectives offertes par le projet Simandou rendent désormais crédible la réflexion sur la création d'un fonds souverain. Selon lui, les importants revenus attendus de l'exploitation du gigantesque gisement de fer pourraient fournir les ressources nécessaires à l'alimentation d'un tel mécanisme. Pour les différents intervenants, la réussite d'un futur fonds souverain dépendra toutefois moins de l'ampleur des recettes minières que de leur gestion, de la qualité de la gouvernance et du respect des meilleures pratiques internationales, afin que les richesses naturelles se traduisent durablement par le développement économique et social de la Guinée.

items.title: Two sets of laws for two sets of people in Ghana – Godfred Dame on Sedina Tamakloe case
items.description: Former Attorney-General and Minister for Justice, Godfred Yeboah Dame, has criticised what he describes as the growing perception that Ghana’s justice system operates “two sets of laws for two sets of people” following the acquittal and discharge of former MASLOC Chief Executive, Sedina Tamakloe Attionu. In a press release issued on Friday July 31, 2026, the former Attorney-General argued that the Court of Appeal’s decision has deepened public concerns over whether political affiliation now influences accountability within Ghana’s criminal justice system. Beyond the acquittal itself, Dame contended that the development fits what he described as a broader pattern in the conduct of criminal prosecutions. He alleged that the current Attorney-General has shown a tendency to discontinue cases involving leading members and affiliates of the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC), while opposition figures continue to face prosecution in corruption-related cases. Referring to the public reaction to the Court of Appeal’s decision, Godfred Dame maintained that the criticism surrounding Sedina Attionu’s acquittal was understandable. He argued that the prosecution had led cogent evidence during the trial, evidence which, according to him, had been widely reported by the media and was therefore well known to the public. The former Attorney-General further asserted that the Sedina case has reinforced the perception that equality before the law is no longer applied evenly. In his view, the principle now exists “only in theory”, warning that confidence in the justice system suffers when citizens believe justice is administered differently depending on political affiliation. Dame also took aim at what he described as the government’s prosecutorial priorities. He argued that Ghanaians should expect higher standards from an administration which, according to him, discontinued criminal cases involving some of its leading members upon assuming office, while subsequently embarking on prosecutions of leading opposition figures under what he characterised as difficult trial conditions. While expressing those concerns, Dame rejected attempts by NDC communicators to attribute Sedina Attionu’s acquittal to the previous Akufo-Addo administration. He maintained that neither he nor the Office of the Attorney-General was served with any notice of appeal during his tenure and insisted that the appeal only became active after the change of government. To support that position, Dame recounted that his principal focus as Attorney-General was not an appeal but the enforcement of the High Court’s judgment. He disclosed that his office successfully pursued Attionu’s extradition from the United States, noting that a United States District Court upheld Ghana’s extradition request in April 2026. Concluding his statement, Mr Dame cautioned that a justice system in which political allies allegedly avoid accountability while political opponents struggle to have their rights respected reflects poorly on the State. He stressed that public confidence in the administration of justice can only be preserved if the law is applied fairly, consistently and without regard to political affiliation.
