items.title: Joy and pain – celebrating Nubuke Foundation at 20
items.description: In today’s world where we are incessantly bombarded with visual imagery wherever we go, one tends to overlook the power of sound. Audio experiences have been overshadowed, yet we shouldn’t forget their ability to subtly transport a listener into another person’s world- while they share stories and memories of joy, pain, events and many more. In the past couple of months, I have had the honour of sharing my thoughts, vision and memories of the journey as a co-founder of Nubuke Foundation. The first steps of this journey actually began almost 25 years ago. I had the pleasure of speaking with Florence Amerley Adu on her Glocal podcast on a rainy morning in Accra, recalling who, why, how, and where Nubuke Foundation? I was reminded of the days when we kept diaries. A peek into your diaries vividly brought the past back, and you disappeared into another world of memories, laughing at things long forgotten or saddened by losses along the way. Listen to my conversation with Florence here: https://lnkd.in/exgPugvA My second conversation with Michelle Renee Jackson (https://lnkd.in/exSkGDBQ ), however, turned out to be a pleasant surprise. It was again an honour to be the first guest from Africa to be interviewed on the Black Philanthropy podcast. Even though I don’t usually refer to myself as a philanthropist, what stood out for me as we began to delve and share stories is how much humankind has in common. I came away from this conversation feeling closer to the African American community – who always seem so far away across the Atlantic – than ever before. Michelle’s thoughtful questions highlighted and opened up into the world of philanthropy, stressing why it mattered. As we are all connected to the bigger picture, we must recognise that every action we take will always have an impact on the community in which we belong and even beyond. What impact or legacy do you choose to leave in your society? My conversation with Michelle can be listened to here: https://lnkd.in/e-A2M7pV Nubuke Foundation’s 20-year legacy is visible in the visual arts and culture of Ghana and worldwide. Happy listening. If you are moved by our story, do get in touch, because our work is not yet done. Philanthropists need philanthropists too! About Nubuke Foundation Nubuke Foundation is a prominent visual art and cultural institution located at 7 Lome Close in East Legon, Accra, Ghana. Established in April 2006 by Odile Tevie, Kofi Tutu Agyare, and Kofi Setordji, it serves as a dynamic creative hub dedicated to preserving, recording, and promoting contemporary art, heritage, and culture in Ghana. For more information about our anniversary programme in October, follow our socials: Instagram: nubuke_foundation | Facebook: Nubuke Foundation | LinkedIn: Nubuke Foundation – The author is Odile Tevie , Co-Founder and Director of Nubuke Foundation.

items.title: WestJet flight attendants go on strike after talks fall through, grounding flights
items.description: Flight attendants at Canada’s WestJet went on strike on Sunday ‌after failing to reach a deal with the country’s second-largest carrier, grounding flights during the busy summer travel season. The Canadian Union of Public Employees, which represents 4,400 flight attendants at the carrier, majority-owned by Onex Corp, is seeking pay ​for its members from the time they check in until they clock out, which is ​not currently the case. The strike follows a four-day work stoppage by flight attendants last August ⁠at larger rival Air Canada, highlighting broader efforts by flight attendants in Canada and the U.S. ​to challenge a compensation structure that mostly pays cabin crew when an aircraft is in motion. The union ​had given 72 hours’ notice on Thursday to the airline signaling that a strike could come if talks failed to produce an agreement, following which WestJet issued a lock-out notice. The union on Sunday said it had tried until the last minute ​to reach a deal but that “WestJet’s offer did not go far enough.” “We are on strike because ​we believe we deserve better. We are ready to go back to the table to settle,” said Alia Hussain, president ‌of ⁠the union’s WestJet component. The airline, which has a domestic market share of about 30%, confirmed the work stoppage and said it would refund or reaccommodate affected passengers. “We presented a proposal… to offer an hourly rate covering all time before and after flights, plus a double-digit wage increase in year one among other priorities the ​union raised. Unfortunately, it ​wasn’t accepted,” WestJet CEO ⁠Alexis von Hoensbroech said. Patty Hajdu, Canada’s jobs minister, described the development as disappointing. “A strike or lockout does not mean an agreement can’t be reached; the ​expectation is that parties can and should come to an agreement at the ​bargaining table,” she ⁠added. The airline canceled 309 flights through Sunday night in anticipation of the strike. It did so to “minimize the risk of stranding guests and aircraft.” The Canadian government intervened to stop the Air Canada strike last year, which was ⁠later defied ​by flight attendants. The union’s WestJet division said it hoped ​the Canadian government would not interfere in the bargaining process.

items.title: Bodies of Nepalese climber Nirmal Purja, 3 other mountaineers recovered on Broad Peak: Alpine Club
items.description: GILGIT: The bodies of celebrated Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and three other mountaineers accompanying him on a summit of the Broad Peak mountain in Gilgit-Baltistan were recovered on Sunday — three days after all 10 members of the team were reported missing after an avalanche. On Saturday, his expedition organising company Elite Exped announced that all members of the team, which also included Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi, had died. The bodies of three climbers were recovered by then, as well as the remains believed to be of a climber from the United States, Naila Kiani of the ACP told Dawn on Sunday. Meanwhile, the ACP announced in a statement that Purja’s body had been found. “The Alpine Club of Pakistan shares this update with profound sorrow. The ground rescue team has reached Nirmal Purja ‘Nims Dai’ at approximately 5,700m on Broad Peak, where three additional bodies have also been sighted, though their identities remain unconfirmed. The ground team will bring the bodies down to the Japanese camp. “Recovery efforts continue under extremely difficult terrain conditions. This information reflects preliminary field reports and remains subject to further confirmation. We urge the public to await official updates before sharing unverified details,” the statement said. View this post on Instagram In a subsequent post, the organisation said three other bodies, identified as China’s Wang Zhong and Nepal’s Nima Sherpa and Kili Pemba Sherpa, had also been recovered. The “four identified climbers are currently being brought down to Camp 1 (C1) and downwards by the ground rescue team,” the post said. View this post on Instagram It said ACP continued to monitor the ongoing recovery operation on Broad Peak, and rescuers had also “confirmed the presence of one additional body at a significantly higher elevation”. However, “due to the extremely hazardous terrain and prevailing conditions, it is unlikely that a recovery attempt will be made at this stage,” it added. Prior to the announcements, ACP General Secretary Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that the ground rescue team was heading towards the advanced base camp on the mountain to carry out the operation. He said that the mountain’s terrain, risk of avalanches and steep slopes were posing challenges in the way of rescue efforts, adding that helicopters could not be employed due to weather conditions. Later, the ACP said in a statement that an eight-member ground team, comprising climbers from Pakistan and Nepal, reached Camp 1 (C1) before 9am. “They will conduct a search and recovery mission on the slopes of Broad Peak under extremely difficult conditions,” the statement added. View this post on Instagram Purja’s expedition team included 10 members, including him. Six of them were Nepalese while there was one each from Pakistan, Oman, the US and China. The bodies of two climbers, Oman’s Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy and Nepal’s Pur Bahadur Gurung, were recovered on Friday, as well as the remains believed to be of American climber Sarah Mallory Geis. On Saturday, the body of Nepal’s Gyalu Sherpa was also recovered, ACP President Irfan Arshad told Dawn . Kiani told Dawn that on Saturday, five other bodies were also spotted on Broad Peak through aerial reconnaissance. Rising 8,051 metres, Broad Peak is the world’s 12th-highest mountain and a technically difficult climb. Seven years before setting out to summit it, Purja had climbed Annapurna, the 10th-highest mountain in the world, in 2019. He then began taking on other 8,000-metre peaks. He set a record for the fastest ascent of the world’s 14 highest mountains, completing the feat in six months in 2019. He became widely known internationally after the Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, ‘14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible’, was released two years later. The 43-year-old climber also served in the British military with the Gurkhas and ​later in special forces. Elite climbers said Purja was a “charismatic, colourful” character. “If we talk about his ​legacy, it’s hard not to focus on how he was at the forefront of shaking up the high altitude guiding,” British climber Kenton Cool, who has climbed Everest 20 ​times, the most by a non-Sherpa, told Reuters on Saturday. In its announcement of the rescue team reaching Purja’s body, the ACP remembered him as a “man who made the impossible possible”. “He carried the Nepali flag to the highest points on Earth with pride, and his achievements brought new recognition to Nepal’s climbing community […] But his impact reached far beyond any one nation, more than the records themselves, he gave people everywhere a reason to believe that the impossible was simply something no one had dared attempt hard enough yet, inspiring dreamers and climbers across the globe to chase what once seemed unreachable.” The statement said, “His loss on the very mountains he so loved is a devastating blow to the global mountaineering family. But his legacy of pushing limits, of proving that the impossible is only impossible until someone dares to do it, will endure in every climber, everywhere, who follows the trail he blazed. “Our deepest condolences go out to his family, loved ones, and the entire climbing community during this immensely difficult time. Rest well, Nims Dai.” Additional input from Reuters

items.title: Dakar vidé de son monde
items.description: À quelques heures du Grand Magal de Touba, célébré ce dimanche 2 août, Dakar retient son souffle. Entre des bus introuvables suite au départ des chauffeurs et le campus de l’Ucad totalement désertés, la capitale tourne au ralenti, vidée d'une grande partie de ses habitants. L’asphalte brûle sous le soleil pesant de ce début du mois d'août, mais à l’arrêt de bus situé juste devant le grand immeuble EMG, la chaleur est le cadet des soucis de la dizaine de personnes amassées sous l'abri délavé. Les yeux rivés vers l’horizon, guettant le moindre reflet d’un bus «Tata», l'impatience se lit sur les visages. Moussa, sac à dos lourdement chargé sur les épaules, consulte sa montre pour la énième fois. Cela fait près d’une trentaine de minutes qu’il attend avec son ami Ahmed pour rejoindre Ouakam. La ligne 67, d'ordinaire si fréquente, semble avoir disparu des radars. « Boy, je ne crois pas qu’on va quitter ici de sitôt… En cette période, presque tous les chauffeurs sont à Touba. C’est toujours la même galère pour trouver une voiture à la veille du Magal, » lâche Moussa en essuyant une goutte de sueur sur son front. Son camarade Ahmed, adossé contre un poteau, secoue la tête d'un air résigné. L'usure de l'attente a fini par entamer son optimisme. « C’est l’effet du Magal, mon frère, lui rétorque-t-il. À mon avis, le mieux c’est qu'on prenne le premier car « Ndiaga Ndiaye » qui passe jusqu’à l’École Normale. On verra bien là-bas si la chance nous sourit davantage. » Comme eux, des milliers de Dakarois se heurtent au ralentissement des transports urbains. Les rabatteurs habituels se font rares, et les quelques véhicules en circulation sont pris d’assaut avant même d’avoir marqué l’arrêt complet. La raison est la grande transhumance vers la capitale du mouridisme pour commémorer le départ en exil de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. À l’Ucad, le grand déménagement En cette matinée du samedi 01 août, après une nuit pluvieuse, les allées de l’Université Cheikh Anta Diop (Ucad) offrent un spectacle encore plus saisissant. Le poumon académique du pays, d’ordinaire grouillant d’une foule compacte et bruyante, s’enfonce dans un silence presque irréel. Dans le campus social du Coud, l’ambiance est aux adieux et aux valises que l'on boucle à la hâte. Ce dimanche marque la fermeture officielle des pavillons pour les grandes vacances. Pour les étudiants résidents, l’obligation de libérer les lieux s’est télescopée avec l’agenda du magal. Devant le pavillon A, des montagnes de bagages, de matelas et de sachets attachés s'entassent sur le trottoir. Les étudiants sont visiblement partagés entre deux logiques, deux itinéraires. Madou, étudiant en Faculté des Lettres, tente d'attacher solidement sa valise avant de le mettre dans le mâle d'un taxi. Pour lui, la destination ne faisait aucun doute. « Pour nous qui sommes mourides, la question ne se pose même pas. On vide la chambre, on pose les affaires chez un parent à Dakar s'il le faut, et on prend la route de Touba. C'est un rendez-vous spirituel qu'on ne peut pas rater. On rentrera dans nos villages respectifs après les cérémonies, » confie-t-il, le visage illuminé par l'enthousiasme du départ. Pour d’autres, en revanche, la fermeture du campus marque simplement le signal du retour au bercail après une éprouvante année universitaire. C’est le cas d’Awa, originaire de Tambacounda, qui attend un véhicule pour la gare routière des Beaux Maraîchers. « Entre la hausse des prix des transports due au Magal et la fermeture des résidences, c'était la course contre la montre ce matin. La majorité de mes voisines de chambre résident à Thiès, pas loin d’ici, mais moi je rentre directement retrouver ma famille dans le Sud-Est. Le campus est tellement vide aujourd'hui, ça fait presque bizarre », confie Awa avec un lot de bagages à ses côtés. Une capitale au repos forcé Au fil des heures, Dakar continue de se délester de ses habitants. Les grandes artères d'habitude embouteillées se désengorgent peu à peu, laissant place à une circulation fluide, presque fantomatique par endroits. Les commerces baissent le rideau les uns après les autres, leurs propriétaires ayant certainement, eux aussi pris la route nationale pour le grand magal. Jusqu’au lundi, la capitale vivra au ralenti, comme suspendue au seul chant des oiseaux dans les différents coins de la capitale. Pour ceux qui restent, il faudra composer avec les services réduits et la quiétude soudaine d'une ville désertée. Djibril DIAO

items.title: 98 enfants égarés pris en charge par la Croix-Rouge, 90 déjà réunis avec leurs familles
items.description: Au-delà de la couverture sanitaire du Grand Magal de Touba 2026, la Croix-Rouge sénégalaise poursuit une mission essentielle. Elle prend en charge les enfants égarés dans la ville sainte. À la date du 1er août, 98 enfants séparés de leurs proches avaient été accueillis par la commission de prise en charge des enfants en situation difficile. Parmi eux, 90 ont déjà pu retrouver leurs parents grâce au dispositif de rétablissement des liens familiaux, selon un communiqué de la Croix-Rouge. Installée devant le domicile de Serigne Fallou Mbacké, cette commission, animée par une quinzaine de volontaires de la Croix-Rouge sénégalaise, a enregistré 128 déclarations de disparition d'enfants, communément appelés. Les équipes poursuivent les recherches afin de permettre aux enfants restants de regagner leurs familles dans les meilleurs délais. Cette mission s'inscrit dans le vaste dispositif déployé par la Croix-Rouge sénégalaise pour le Grand Magal. Au total, 448 secouristes sont mobilisés sur 29 sites de prestations de santé à travers Touba. Les volontaires interviennent dans les hôpitaux, les centres de santé, les postes médicaux avancés, au péage Ila Touba, auprès de plusieurs foyers religieux ainsi qu'autour de la Grande Mosquée, où une équipe mobile prend en charge les pèlerins les plus vulnérables. Selon le secrétaire général du comité départemental de la Croix-Rouge de Mbacké, Modou Diop, les équipes ont également assuré plusieurs évacuations sanitaires grâce à une ambulance médicalisée et deux véhicules d'intervention. Rien que le samedi 1er août, 116 pèlerins ont été assistés au poste de secours du péage Ila Touba et 336 patients ont été pris en charge à l'hôpital Ndamatou. Modou Diop a salué l'engagement des volontaires et les a invités à poursuivre leurs interventions dans le respect des principes humanitaires. Il a rappelé que le comité départemental de la Croix-Rouge de Mbacké a participé à l'ensemble des préparatifs du Grand Magal, notamment aux réunions de coordination, aux opérations de nettoiement, aux caravanes « 18 Safar », à la formation des premiers répondants et aux actions de sensibilisation. Birane DIOP (Correspondant)

items.title: A Rodeo That Reminds Me of Home
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Yvonne Wingett Sanchez, a staff writer who’s covered the fight over who runs elections in Maricopa County , the arc of the Voting Rights Act , and why election deniers are winning . Yvonne has a nostalgic fondness for state fairs and rodeos, and she’s excited for an upcoming one in her home state. She also recommends watching anything with Billy Bob Thornton in it, reading Chris Whitaker for a good mystery, and putting down the hair crimper in the year 2026. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor The upcoming event I’m most looking forward to: The Hondo Rodeo Fest in Phoenix, where I’ll watch the Turnpike Troubadours sing and the cowboys compete in everything from bull riding to barrel racing. I grew up going to rodeos and competing in county cooking showcases in small-town Idaho, and even though I’ve lived in Arizona for decades, a big piece of my heart still considers Idaho home. Every now and then, I hit the county rodeos outside of Phoenix because the smells, the riders, the announcers, the food on a stick, and the leather-fringe rodeo chaps all remind me of my childhood. I’ve never been to the Hondo Rodeo Fest before, and my husband—who grew up in a small town near Fort Worth, Texas, and is always looking for an excuse to wear his boots—made plans for us to try the big-city rodeo scene. We can’t wait! The television show I’m most enjoying right now: My guilty pleasure is watching The Real Housewives , and I am loving the new Rhode Island series. (Rosie is my favorite!) I also can’t get enough of the twists and turns of British crime dramas, and I plan on rewatching Jed Mercurio’s Line of Duty (which has been on hiatus) before the next season premieres. An actor I would watch in anything: Billy Bob Thornton. He seems to effortlessly channel a variety of complicated, unpredictable, and funny characters. He has a way of making you root for him, even when he’s skirting—or completely breaking—all the rules. I grew up watching him in Westerns with my dad ( The Alamo and Tombstone ), and he was brilliant in Sling Blade . I’ve loved him in everything since, including Goliath , Landman , and yes, even Bad Santa . A quiet song that I love: I can’t stop listening to Flatland Cavalry, a country band from Lubbock, Texas, that a friend introduced me to last summer. Their ballad “Mountain Song” takes me back to my childhood in the Mountain West, where I’d spend summer evenings on the back porch of our apple orchard. Our home had a breathtaking view of the area’s towering butte, which resembles a woman’s face, and the song reminds me of my parents, nature, and a simpler time. A musical artist who means a lot to me: Willie Nelson. He’s part of my core childhood memories. My family spent hours trekking in our motor home to Idaho campsites, the beaches of the Pacific Northwest, and the parking lots of Las Vegas casinos (Circus Circus, anyone?). Those road trips almost always featured my dad behind the wheel, the window half down while he sang along to “On the Road Again” and “To All the Girls I’ve Loved Before.” (My mom, on the other hand, preferred “Always on My Mind.”) Best novel I’ve recently read, and the best work of nonfiction: I love a good mystery, and All the Colors of the Dark , by Chris Whitaker, drew me in for days. Beginning in small-town Missouri in the 1970s, it follows a serial killer and a missing-person case. The story is so gripping and well written, I didn’t want it to end. When it did, I bought all of Whitaker’s other books, which are piled up on my nightstand. As for nonfiction, I just binged Regime Change , a new chronicle of the first year of President Trump’s second term, by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. It’s exceptional—and the reporting is jaw-dropping. A cultural product I loved as a teenager and still love: I discovered Selena’s Tejano music when I was in middle school, danced to “Bidi Bidi Bom Bom” throughout high school, and still listen to her rancheras today. (It was an honor to spend time with her dad and sister back in 2005 for a story I wrote about the 10-year anniversary of her death.) Something I loved but now dislike: Hair crimpers. Love the look, don’t miss the smell of burning hair. A piece of me dies every time I watch my daughter straighten her natural curls, only to singe zigzag shapes into her hair. A favorite story I’ve read in The Atlantic : “ The Missing Kayaker ,” by Jamie Thompson. It is an irresistible—and infuriating—mystery. Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: My 11-year-old daughter is obsessed with the Athletes Unlimited Softball League, the new women’s professional softball league, and I’m obsessed now too. Our favorite player is Bri Ellis, who plays first base for the Utah Talons. She is kind, funny, strong, and an inspiration for young girls and the moms raising them. The last thing that made me cry: I’m going to go full mom here. A few weeks ago, we were up in Prescott, Arizona, for a softball tournament. The weather was perfect, and the bases were loaded, with two outs in the last inning. My daughter had two strikes on her and then nailed the ball out to left field for the game-winning hit. I bawled as she rounded first base and then was mobbed at second base by a sweaty mess of preteen girls celebrating their win. A quote that I return to: I often recall this 1944 diary passage by Anne Frank, which perfectly encapsulates hope for humanity: “It’s really a wonder that I haven’t dropped all my ideals, because they seem so absurd and impossible to carry out. Yet I keep them, because in spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart.” The Week Ahead Tony , a biopic that follows Anthony Bourdain as he begins his career in the restaurant world (in select theaters Friday) Etna , a novel by Paul Yoon told through the eyes of an ex-military dog returning home after war (out Tuesday) The Shards , a series adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel, set at an elite Los Angeles prep school in 1981 (out Wednesday on Hulu) Essay Illustration by The Atlantic Is This What Comes After AI Slop? By Will Oremus Among thousands of self-published Amazon ebooks that they identified as containing “substantial AI text,” none was more popular than Daggermouth . Until recently, AI fiction has been easy to dismiss as slop. On Amazon, new-book releases nearly tripled from 2022 to 2025. (That’s probably not because humans suddenly dedicated themselves en masse to the written word.) Many are blatant copycats of existing titles, seemingly intended to trick readers into buying them. Their sales figures are generally meager; the reviews, indignant. A suspicious number of them feature protagonists with the same names . Last year, readers of one fantasy novel noticed a line that seemed to be responding to a prompt asking a chatbot to write in the style of another author. But if a book as beloved as Daggermouth were written with a chatbot, it would raise an awkward question: Could AI fiction be getting … good? Read the full article. items.title: Taking Care of the Father Who Broke My Heart
items.description: A few hours after Levi Fishback died last month, at a nursing home in Kentucky, the funeral director called me. She needed to know whether the family wanted an open casket. What songs would Levi have wanted? What color flowers? Who should give the eulogies? By now I should be used to being asked questions about my father that I don’t know the answers to. I spent the past four years as his medical proxy, the only family member responsible for handling the bills from the nursing home and overseeing his care. But I barely knew the man. I felt uncomfortable deciding whether the nurses should give him a flu shot every fall, let alone choosing what to put in his obituary. I needed to include photos, but I had only one: from my fourth or fifth birthday. I messaged his ex-wife and the stepdaughter he’d raised, along with my half brother’s two children, for more, and they delivered, sending photos of my dad—smiling widely in a suit and tie—alongside them at graduations and family parties. I didn’t know that he’d had that much joy inside of him. My memories of my dad are like a few scatterplots on the graph of my life. He had lived right across town from me in Lexington, Kentucky, but he would go months without visiting me. From the ages of 10 to 14, I don’t think I saw him a single time. He had his own family—his wife, his stepdaughter, and his son from a previous relationship. When he and his wife got married, his son was the ring bearer and her daughter was the flower girl. I wasn’t a flower girl at the wedding. I didn’t go to the wedding. I didn’t even know about the wedding. They had a piano in their living room that his stepdaughter played. She is a year older than me and went to a rival high school. I would see her sometimes—she was a cheerleader, and she had all the name-brand clothes that the pretty, popular girls wore. My mom, Trina, was addicted to crack for years and had struggled to take care of me and her four younger kids. Levi must have known it. Once, when I was about 7 or 8, he came to my mom’s door. It had been a bad week, or a bad few weeks. My mom had gone out—I’m not sure when or where—and I was alone with my four little brothers and sisters. Our refrigerator was empty. Dirty plates and clothes lay around, broken toys all over the place. We were untamed children who did what we wanted—my brother Colby was always trying to do backflips off the arm of the couch. [ Read: Jenisha from Kentucky ] Maybe my dad had heard on the streets that Trina’s kids needed help. Or maybe it was a random visit. I was jittery when we opened the door to him. He was a short man with thick eyebrows that dominated his face, but in our eyes, he was a hero. We knew he would help us, because drugs didn’t control his life; he wasn’t damaged like Trina; he was a man who took care of a wife and children. He would recognize our fear and desperation. He stepped inside but stayed close to the door. He looked around like one of the social workers the government sometimes sent, and we huddled around him, watching him judge the mess with his eyes. And then he left. He said he’d come back for me, but he didn’t . Plenty of people my age are beginning to take care of sick or aging parents. It’s the natural way; you take care of the people who once took care of you. You don’t resent it, because now you’re the strong one, and they’re the vulnerable one, and you owe them everything. But for me, it wasn’t like that. W hen I was 9, I was sent to stay with my aunts. While I was gone, the state took my siblings away from Trina; my sister went to an aunt and my brothers were put in foster care. I moved back to Lexington for the fifth grade, and my grandmother took me in—I don’t remember anyone ever suggesting that I could stay with my father. I have one memory of him from that year I came back: For some reason, he showed up at my school and found me in the lunch line. He handed me some money and then pulled me toward him for a hug. I was embarrassed by his affection and don’t think I embraced him back. I lived with my grandmother until I graduated from high school. Levi would call sometimes. “Jenisha, get the phone. It’s yo daddy,” she’d shout. I’d rush to the phone—toddler-excited to hear from him. A call from my father was like Christmas. Sometimes he’d ask if I wanted him to pick me up the next day, and so I’d spend hours waiting for him to drive up the driveway. Occasionally he would actually show, but usually he wouldn’t. Once, in middle school, I spent a weekend with him and his wife. I made up a lie: I told his wife that I’d skipped a grade in elementary school. I wanted her to like me and think I was smart; I didn’t think it was a big deal. But a few hours after he’d dropped me back off at my grandmother’s, he called me. He’d found out about the lie and gave me a long lecture, and then a punishment: “You can’t come over here no more,” he told me. I was surprised he was angry. After all, he lied to me all the time—about being on his way to pick me up, about how he would drop off spending money for my field trip or take me back-to-school shopping. But this time he stuck to his word: I didn’t hear from him for a few years after that. A month before I graduated from college, in 2008, I was in an evening class when he called my cellphone. He and his wife had gotten divorced by then. I stepped out to the hallway to answer. He was calling to tell me that he had a condition, and his doctor said there was a test I could take to see whether I had the “same gene.” He didn’t say what it was, and I didn’t ask any follow-up questions, because he swiftly changed the subject. “You graduating?” he asked, although he knew the answer. I wasn’t surprised when he didn’t ask about the details of the ceremony. He just spouted some compliments: “Man, you graduating. You good with that English. You gotta be real smart to do English in school.” He hadn’t come to my high-school graduation, and he didn’t come to this one, either. I graduated, packed my bags, and left Kentucky to move to New York City. I was building a new life, and I thought about him only when a guy dumped me. If my own father thought I was worthless and didn’t want to stay in my life, how could I expect a romantic partner to want me? I measured my value by his absence. Illustration by Vanessa Saba. Source: Jenisha Watts. Sometimes he’d send me a corny text, something that I couldn’t imagine him ever actually saying: “I love you like a fat kid loves cake,” he wrote once. I treated it like spam. I didn’t see him again until 2015. By then he had moved to an assisted-living place and was using a walker to get around. His speech was slurred, and his hands shook. I took him out to the all-you-can-eat buffet at Golden Corral. Most of the time, he just smiled, showing his chipped and missing teeth. Later, I heard that his illness was getting worse and that my half brother was taking care of him. I never quite knew why my brother had lived with our dad and I hadn’t. Maybe Levi was just proud to have a son, and what he felt about me was shame—shame that he was connected to a woman like my mom, a crack addict. Lexington is a small town, and Levi never smoked or used drugs. He’d always claimed that my mom was a one-night stand. But my brother had his own problems. He was involved in selling drugs, and then in 2022, he disappeared. He told me one thing before he left: “Now it’s your turn.” I had questions about Levi’s bills and care, but no one could reach my brother. I understood why last year, when he was apprehended and sent to Blackburn Correctional Complex. He’d been on the run from the Lexington police—wanted for trafficking cocaine, fleeing or evading police, and possessing a firearm. As far as I know he was in touch with Levi only once in those years, when he texted my dad’s ex-wife a message for our dad, and she shared the message with me: “Tell him I said I love him and miss him.” I read that message over and over again, wondering what it would be like to love our dad and miss him. Obviously, my brother knew a different side of Levi. I wanted to love him, too, but it was like trying to touch the air. Yet if I didn’t take care of him, who would? [ Read: Dear Therapist: I don’t want to take care of my aging, homophobic parents ] At times, I resented my brother for what he’d had in the past, and for not being around now. Like when the nursing home called to say there had been “a little smoke incident with one of our dryers and the fire department came here to evacuate.” Or when a nurse left me a voicemail: “Just checking in for the care-plan meeting.” I resented him, and I resented Levi. But I called the nurse back. I went to the meetings. Whenever I went back to Kentucky, I made a point to visit my father. But I didn’t do any more than I felt I had to. I thought of Levi sometimes as a stranger sleeping at a bus stop. The idea of walking away from him felt cruel—but also liberating. I once wasn’t able to care for myself, and walked away from me too. L evi was a professional gambler who shot dice and bet on horses. He spent most of his time at the Red Mile Racetrack wagering on standardbreds galloping around the track, or on the simulcast of races around the country that played inside. He took me a few times when I was little, and I remember him staring at the screen, like an airline traveler scanning for their final destination. But most of what I know about Levi I know from other people. When people learned that he was my father, they always had a story to tell. His nickname was Sonny, and he earned real money at the track, sometimes leaving with bundles of cash. I’ve heard stories of him handing out crisp $100 bills like Monopoly money, or treating a group to breakfast after winning. He was also known to cheat at dice sometimes, by playing with altered dice. He was estranged from his brother and sister. Their youngest brother had killed himself when he was 18. He’d used Levi’s pistol to do it, and my surviving uncle, Kenny, never forgave him for it. Kenny has told me a little more over the years. Levi ran track even though he was “a short motherfucker,” he told me—which interested me, because I was a runner too, and I was fast. I always wondered where I’d got it from. The truth is Kenny couldn’t stand him. “Your daddy ain’t shit,” he’d say. “It seems like a man would look out for his daughter.” More recently, I learned about Levi from his nurses. His favorite soda was Pepsi. He loved soft sweets, such as an oatmeal pie. And last year, during a meeting with his care team, I finally learned what his diagnosis was: a form of cerebellar ataxia, a degenerative neurological condition that can be inherited. I thought back to that call from so many years ago, when he had told me I could take a genetic test to find out whether I was at risk. But I didn’t take the test. I still haven’t. I’m afraid. And the last thing I want to think about is whether we share the same gene. I saw him in April, when I had to fly back to Kentucky for the funeral of another family member. The drive to the nursing home was long, and I was glad—it gave me time to prepare to see this man who was almost a stranger to me. I passed old gas stations, homes with acres of grass, a fresh eggs for sale sign hanging on a residential mailbox. I thought about how I didn’t know the sound of his laugh, how I wouldn’t have been able to describe his voice. The woman at the front desk greeted me: “Hi, Jenisha.” The other nurses just called me “Levi’s daughter.” They probably assumed we had a normal relationship, that he was a normal parent, and here I was, their patient’s “loved one,” doing my normal duty. “You’re the only person who comes to see him,” a nurse told me. Maybe she was trying to make me feel proud. But I just felt sad. His ex-wife and stepdaughter visited now and then, but not regularly. Where were all of the people he’d been close with in Kentucky? How was I the only one there, when he was notorious for breaking my heart? I walked to his room, which he shared with another man, a curtain dividing the space. The television was on—an old black-and-white cowboy movie—but there was no sound. The person in the bed was nothing like the Levi from my childhood, slick-talking and arrogant. He was fragile and could barely lift his head up. He struggled to drink from a straw, and I watched as his mouth kept missing the hole. Sitting beside him, I dug for emotion, wanting to feel what another kind of daughter would feel. I felt like I was in a movie myself, an actress in a father-daughter scene. Kisses on my forehead. Talks about my first boyfriend. My daddy—who saw me as the most beautiful girl in the world—always wanted his darling daughter close to him. “Don’t leave,” he’d say. “Stay as long as you want.” But all I really felt was nervous. Even though my father couldn’t speak or stand, even though he had shrunk to 77 pounds and was smaller than I was, being near him still turned me back into that scared little girl hoping for scraps. At one point I asked: “Do you love me? Nod your head if you do.” He responded by moving his head up and down. Watching him use up all of his strength to answer me filled me with a childlike high. At last, he wasn’t going to reject me anymore. But only a few minutes later, he lifted his hand and flapped it at me. He made the gesture again. I realized he was shooing me away. I couldn’t believe it. “Are you ready for me to leave?” I asked. He nodded yes. Even at his most vulnerable, even when he was utterly alone in the world, he was still turning me away. L ast month, the nursing home called at 4:39 a.m. “He died peacefully,” the nurse told me. The day before, I’d talked to Levi on FaceTime and I saw how sunken he looked. Even as he was transitioning, I had little to say to him. “I love you. Are you ready to see your mom?” He nodded. [ Read: Americans are in denial about elder care ] I arranged for other family members to FaceTime, too, and the prison helped set up a call for my brother. The nurse told me that they both were crying. I kept asking her: “Did you tell him that I made it happen? What did my brother say?” My ego wanted them to know that I had made the call possible. I pictured both of them crying. All I could think was: Damn, I wish I could feel what my brother was feeling . We scheduled the funeral for July 3, two days after my brother would be released from prison. I decided against the open casket. Levi’s body was twisted into the fetal position. To get him into an open casket, the funeral director told me, she’d have to break his legs, arms, and fingers. “I don’t want to do that to Levi,” she said. For weeks, I couldn’t decide whether or not to go to the funeral. My mom said I shouldn’t feel like I had to: “Levi didn’t show up for a lot of things for you,” she reminded me. Paying my respects seemed like the right thing to do. But more than that, a part of me wanted to prove that I was the bigger person. I wanted others—his family, his stepdaughter—to lay eyes on me, and to see that I’d made something of myself in spite of his absence. I wanted them to know that I’d been his emergency contact, the one who took care of him in the end. But the day before, I stayed home. I decided that I would watch it on Facebook Live. The truth is that I wasn’t mourning my father; I was grieving the loss of what I’d never had. I didn’t cry when he died. But when I heard the speech that his stepdaughter gave at the funeral, the feelings hit me. Like me, she was a runner, and they used to go on jogs together. Someday, she said, she believed she would see Levi in heaven. “Come on,” he’d tell her, “let’s race,” and off they would go again. She said that Levi left her with many happy moments. And that’s when I cried. I’ll never understand why he didn’t show up in my life, but I have to stop asking. There was a brief chapter of his life when he needed me, a period when he might have recognized me as someone who was important to him. I still wanted to please him, wanted him to see for himself that he’d made a terrible mistake by not being my father. And now that chapter is over.

items.title: Five dead, 41 missing, after Indonesia ferry catches fire
items.description: Five people have been found dead and 41 are missing after an Indonesian ferry carrying at least 250 people caught fire while at sea, officials say. The captain of the ship reported the fire – off Madura island – as the vessel sailed from the country’s second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, to Makassar in South Sulawesi, according to Basarnas, the National Search and Rescue Agency. Footage played by local Indonesian news outlet iNews shows large numbers of people in life jackets on what appears to be a lifeboat. Other clips show people climbing down from the ferry that has flames and plumes of smoke coming from the top of the vessel. Basarnas posted a video to its TikTok, with a statement saying at 08:24 (02:24 GMT) the Surabaya Search and Rescue office received information that passenger ship KMP Mutiara Sentosa 2 was on fire. “Based on information from the shipping company, the fire occurred at around 06:00-07:00 (00:00-01:00 GMT).” Later, Basarnas said it got confirmation the ferry “was almost entirely engulfed in flames” as “passengers held on in the ship’s bridge and bow while awaiting rescue”. In some of the footage, can be seen jumping into the sea, with crowds of people in life jackets gathering and lifebuoys being thrown to some before they are carried into a rescue ship.

items.title: Burkina/Religion : le Soufisme rime avec paix et tolérance religieuse, selon Cheick Moaze Ouédraogo
items.description: Burkina/Religion : le Soufisme rime avec paix et tolérance religieuse, selon Cheick Moaze Ouédraogo Ouagadougou, 1er août 2026 (AIB)-Réélu Président de la Communauté internationale des Soufis(CIS) lors du congrès extraordinaire du 19 juillet 2026 à Ouagadougou, Cheikh Soufi Moaze Ouédraogo a réaffirmé vendredi l’incompatibilité du soufisme avec toute forme d’intolérance religieuse. Dans un communiqué signé le 31 juillet 2026, le guide de la communauté Soufie au Burkina Faso Cheikh Soufi Moaze Ouédraogo a renouvelé l'engagement de son organisation en faveur de la paix, du dialogue et du vivre-ensemble. Selon le président Cheikh Soufi Moaze Ouedraogo, le Soufisme condamne toute forme d’intolérance religieuse, assurant que tout disciple qui s’en prendrait à une personne non musulmane en raison de sa religion serait exclu de la communauté. Il a rappelé que le soufisme est « une école de paix, de fraternité, de respect mutuel et d’acceptation de l’autre ». La CIS a réitéré sa détermination à poursuivre ses actions de sensibilisation, d’éducation spirituelle et de promotion du dialogue afin de contribuer durablement à la paix, à la fraternité, à la cohésion sociale et à la stabilité du Burkina Faso. En rappel, le congres extraordinaire tenu du 18 au 19 juillet 2026 à Ouagadougou a mis en place un bureau national de 35 membres, assisté de deux commissaires aux comptes. La rencontre a réuni des représentants venus de plusieurs localités du Burkina Faso ainsi que de la diaspora. Pour Cheick Ouédraogo, la rencontre a été également une occasion pour promouvoir les valeurs fondamentales du soufisme, notamment la paix, la tolérance, l'acceptation de l'autre, le dialogue interreligieux et intercommunautaire ainsi que la coexistence pacifique. La Communauté Internationale des Soufis renouvelle son attachement au respect de la dignité humaine, à la liberté de conscience, au dialogue entre les religions, à la cohésion sociale et au vivre-ensemble harmonieux au Burkina Faso. Le président réélu a, par ailleurs, exprimé sa reconnaissance aux autorités, aux responsables religieux et coutumiers, aux forces de défense et de sécurité, aux médias, au comité d'organisation ainsi qu'à l'ensemble des participants pour leur contribution au succès du congrès. Agence d’information du Burkina YOS/ata

items.title: Yacine Rahmoun, de la Silicon Valley à l’Algérie : le pari gagnant d’un entrepreneur de la tech
items.description: Né à Alger, passé par la Silicon Valley avant de revenir investir dans son pays, Yacine Rahmoun, 56 ans, revient sur son parcours marqué par l'innovation et l'entrepreneuriat. Cet Algéro-Américain est né et a grandi à Alger, qu'il considère comme le plus bel endroit au monde. Une enfance rythmée par les amis, les journées à la plage, l'école et une passion pour le football. Il débute à l'école de football d'El Biar avant d'intégrer le CR Belouizdad ( CRB), l'un des meilleurs clubs d'Algérie. Ensuite, il est sélectionné pour jouer en équipe nationale. « Porter pour la première fois le maillot vert et blanc de la sélection algérienne a renforcé mon attachement au pays », affirme Yacine Rahmoun. Mais, une blessure met fin brutalement à son parcours de footballeur. Yacine Rahmoun, un entrepreneur de la tech qui mise sur l’Algérie Parmi ses plus beaux souvenirs, Yacine Rahmoun cite la mixité sociale qu'il a connue à Alger. Il évoque une table autour de laquelle se retrouvaient un pilote de ligne, un cafetier, un sportif ou encore un chômeur. Côté études, Après l'obtention de son baccalauréat au lycée Amara Rachid, il effectue une année à l'Université des sciences et de la technologie Houari-Boumediene ( USTHB ), à Bab Ezzouar. « J'y ai acquis des bases solides qui m'ont ensuite permis d'être admis à l'École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), en Suisse », affirme-t-il à TSA. À cette époque, son objectif est clair, revenir en Algérie après ses études, une fois la langue japonaise apprise. Mais son parcours prend une tout autre direction. « Alors que je devais rejoindre Panasonic au Japon, le centre de recherche où j'étais attendu a fermé quelques jours avant mon départ. L'entreprise m'a alors proposé d'intégrer son nouveau laboratoire de recherche en reconnaissance vocale, à Santa Barbara, en Californie » aux Etats-Unis, raconte-t-il. En 1992, il rejoint l'entreprise avant de découvrir San Francisco et la Silicon Valley. « À cette époque, des entreprises comme Apple, Intel, Cisco ou encore Yahoo étaient en plein essor. J'ai été fasciné par cet écosystème d'innovation », poursuit-il. « Je me suis alors dit que j'allais prolonger mon séjour d'un an supplémentaire. Finalement, cette année est devenue vingt ans », ajoute cet Algéro-Américain. Son passage dans la Silicon Valley façonne durablement sa vision de l'entrepreneuriat, dans un environnement où, selon lui, seules les compétences comptent. « J'y ai découvert une culture fondée sur l'innovation, le travail collectif, la prise d'initiative et l'optimisme », explique-t-il. Une expérience qui lui apprend à maîtriser ses émotions, à rester patient, positif et à ne pas prendre les difficultés personnellement. Des qualités qui peuvent paraître simples au premier abord, mais qui sont, selon lui, particulièrement difficiles à acquérir. Une autre philosophie va profondément marquer son parcours : celle du « Receive and Give Back » (« Recevoir et redonner »). « En 1996, Yahoo m'a accordé un premier financement de 5.000 dollars. Lorsque j'ai demandé pourquoi on m'aidait, on m'a répondu : « C'est l'esprit de la Silicon Valley. Un jour, vous aiderez quelqu'un à votre tour » », confie Yacine Rahmoun. Cette philosophie influencera durablement son parcours et son engagement en faveur de l'entrepreneuriat. « Si tu veux aider ton pays, tu dois être sur le terrain » En 2009, il décide, avec plusieurs amis de la Silicon Valley, Algériens comme étrangers attachés à l'Algérie, de contribuer au développement de son pays natal. « Nous avons estimé que nous avions une dette morale envers notre pays. Nous nous sommes demandé ce que nous pouvions faire concrètement pour contribuer à son développement », explique-t-il. Ils choisissent alors de miser sur la technologie, l'innovation et la création de startups en lançant Algerian Startup Initiative (ASI). Ils organisent la première compétition nationale de business plans, accompagnée de bootcamps dans plusieurs universités afin de faire découvrir l'entrepreneuriat aux étudiants. « En quelques semaines, nous avons reçu 145 projets », se souvient-il. Cette expérience leur permet de tirer deux constats. Le premier est que l'Algérie dispose d'un formidable vivier de talents grâce aux investissements réalisés dans l'éducation. Le second est qu'il faut créer davantage d'opportunités économiques afin de retenir ces compétences, faute de quoi elles partiront à l'étranger. En 2010, à l’âge de 40 ans, Yacine décide de revenir s'installer en Algérie avec sa famille pour créer une entreprise dans la technologique, CaptureDoc. « Un ami m'a donné un conseil qui m'a beaucoup marqué : « Si tu veux aider ton pays, tu dois être sur le terrain » ». Convaincu du potentiel de l'Algérie, Yacine Rahmoune franchit le pas, persuadé que contribuer durablement au développement du pays nécessite d'être présent sur le terrain, au contact des entrepreneurs, des entreprises et des projets. « Je me suis aussi beaucoup inspiré du modèle de Singapour, qui a su mobiliser sa diaspora pour accélérer son développement économique. Je n'ai jamais regretté cette décision », assure-t-il. CaptureDoc, une startup algérienne qui exporte ses services Après son installation en Algérie, il fonde CaptureDoc en 2010 avec l'ambition d'accompagner les entreprises dans leur transformation numérique. L'objectif est d'améliorer les processus existants afin de les rendre plus rapides, plus efficaces et moins coûteux, tout en développant de nouveaux services innovants. « Nous avons progressivement constitué une équipe d'ingénieurs de très haut niveau, ce qui nous a permis de déployer des projets de transformation digitale sur quatre continents », fait valoir l'entrepreneur. L'intelligence artificielle occupe aujourd'hui une place centrale dans la stratégie de l'entreprise, qui exporte désormais des solutions développées en Algérie vers des clients internationaux. « Notre plus grande fierté reste d'avoir démontré qu'une entreprise algérienne pouvait innover, exporter son savoir-faire et être récompensée à l'international », se félicite-t-il. CaptureDoc compte aujourd'hui une cinquantaine de collaborateurs, tous Algériens. Plusieurs membres de la diaspora ayant choisi de revenir vivre en Algérie ont également rejoint l'entreprise. « Nos équipes sont multiculturelles et multilingues. Elles travaillent quotidiennement avec des clients en Europe, au Moyen-Orient, en Afrique et en Amérique », explique-t-il. Selon lui, cette diversité constitue un véritable atout pour répondre aux attentes de partenaires internationaux. Au-delà des résultats économiques, sa plus grande satisfaction reste la création d’emplois qualifiés en Algérie. Les conseils de Yacine Rahmoun aux jeunes Pour les jeunes Algériens qui souhaitent suivre un parcours similaire, Yacine Rahmoun conseille avant tout d'être passionné et enthousiaste. « Lorsqu'on est animé par la passion et l'envie de réussir, rien ne peut véritablement nous arrêter », souligne-t-il. Il recommande également de cultiver la patience, l'humilité, une attitude positive et la maîtrise de ses émotions. Au-delà des parcours individuels, Yacine Rahmoun est convaincu que les compétences algériennes, qu'elles vivent en Algérie ou à l'étranger, constituent un véritable levier de développement. Concernant la diaspora, il estime qu'elle a un rôle majeur à jouer dans le développement de l'entrepreneuriat et de l'innovation en Algérie. Selon lui, elle regorge de compétences susceptibles de contribuer au développement de l'économie, de la technologie, de la culture ou encore du sport. « Au-delà de la diaspora, il est tout aussi important de réfléchir à la manière de retenir les talents déjà présents en Algérie », rappelle-t-il. Pour y parvenir, il plaide en faveur d’emplois de qualité, d'une rémunération attractive et d'une meilleure qualité de vie. « Au sein de l'entreprise, nous essayons de créer un environnement dans lequel chacun peut s'épanouir et prendre du plaisir dans son travail », explique-t-il. Yacine Rahmoun appelle également à renforcer le dialogue entre les pouvoirs publics et les entrepreneurs. « Il serait utile de réunir régulièrement les startups, les PME et les grandes entreprises afin d'identifier les principaux freins à leur développement et de construire des solutions communes », recommande-t-il. Enfin, il estime que l'Algérie doit poursuivre ses efforts afin de renforcer son attractivité et d'attirer davantage d'investissements internationaux. Après plus de vingt ans passés aux États-Unis, Yacine Rahmoun assure n'avoir jamais regretté son retour en Algérie. Convaincu que le pays dispose des talents nécessaires pour réussir sa transformation, il estime que le défi consiste désormais à créer les conditions permettant de retenir les compétences, d'attirer les investisseurs et de faire de l'innovation un véritable moteur de développement. L’article Yacine Rahmoun, de la Silicon Valley à l'Algérie : le pari gagnant d'un entrepreneur de la tech est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Afflux de migrants à Ceuta : au moins 90 morts, des clandestins encore présents dans l’enclave
items.description: Dans l'enclave espagnole de Ceuta, ou des dizaines de milliers de migrants ont afflue ces derniers jours, la Guardia civil et les services de secours continuent de faire de macabres decouvertes. Ainsi, ce 2 août au matin, le bilan des victimes s'eleve desormais a 90 morts, selon des annonces de la Delegation du gouvernement a Ceuta reprises par des medias espagnols. « La plupart des corps ont ete retrouves pres de la digue de Tarajal », a precise le journal sportif Marca . « L'hopital, les services d'urgence et le Centre de retention administrative pour migrants (CETI) ont dû faire face a un afflux massif de personnes en quelques heures seulement, tandis que de nombreux migrants, pieds nus, erraient dans les rues en attendant de l'aide », peut-on lire dans ce media, qui evoque egalement le travail des ONG qui actuellement « continuent d'apporter une aide humanitaire aux personnes restees sur place ». Estas son las escalofriantes escenas de esta madrugada en Ceuta que contradicen el relato del Gobierno. Seguir: @elalcazar_es pic.twitter.com/SUGaDve80p — El Alcázar (@elalcazar_es) August 2, 2026 Des individus restes sur place qui semblent ne pas se limiter aux seuls « mineurs » isoles . Si le gouvernement espagnol a annonce le retour de « presque tous » les clandestins au Maroc, des videos circulant sur les reseaux sociaux semblent indiquer le contraire. Au plus fort de la crise, les autorites locales avaient annonce qu'environ 60 000 personnes avaient traverse la frontiere en moins de 24 heures. Une partie de la presse espagnole s'est fait l'echo des avertissements qu'auraient adresses les renseignements au gouvernement quant a l'imminence de cette percee migratoire contre les villes de Ceuta et Melilla alors qu'approchait la Fete du Trone au Maroc. Une fete nationale a l'occasion de laquelle les services espagnols estimaient que le roi Mohammed VI pourrait faire preuve de « magnanimite ».

items.title: Mahama concerned over unhygienic fish drying video at Tema Newtown
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has expressed concern over a video recorded by the Buzstop Boys, showing fish being dried in what he described as unhygienic conditions at Tema Newtown. Speaking at Ringway Gospel Centre Assemblies of God, Mahama said the video, which captured the sanitation situation at the fishing community, revealed the poor environmental conditions under which fish meant for the market was being processed. “The fish is supposed to come into the market. These Buzstop Boys went to Tema Newtown, and if you see the rubbish there, they were drying fish. And that fish is supposed to come into the market,” he said. He said the footage highlights the urgent need for improved sanitation and better management of food processing areas to protect public health. Mahama also commended the work of the Buzstop Boys, a group known for drawing public attention to sanitation challenges through their environmental advocacy activities. The President further urged Ghanaians to adopt responsible waste disposal habits, warning that throwing sachet water wrappers, Styrofoam containers, food packaging and other refuse into drains contributes to flooding. Quoting James 2:17, which states that “faith without works is dead,” Mahama said environmental cleanliness requires action and must be reflected in the behaviour and character of citizens.

items.title: Okyeame Kwame: A true example of a national asset
items.description: In an era where celebrity influence is often measured by social media clout, viral trends, or fleeting moments of fame, few public figures manage to transcend entertainment to become permanent fixtures of national progress. In Ghana, one name stands out as the gold standard of purposeful celebrity: Kwame Nsiah-Apau, universally known as Okyeame Kwame. Earning the title of a “national asset” is no small feat. It requires consistency, unmatched patriotism, intellectual depth, and a career devoid of toxic controversies. With his latest appointment as the Ghana Health Service’s National Hepatitis Ambassador, Okyeame Kwame has once again cemented his place not just as the “Rap Doctor,” but as Ghana’s ultimate civic champion. The Evolution of a Civic Icon For over two decades, Okyeame Kwame has redefined what it means to be a musician in Africa. While his lyrical prowess and timeless discography earned him legendary status in the highlife and hiplife genres, his dedication to social impact has truly set him apart. Governments change, political tides shift, and ministerial portfolios rotate, but Okyeame Kwame remains a constant pillar of trust for state institutions. His journey through various high-profile national portfolios tells the story of a citizen deeply invested in every facet of Ghana’s development: The National Hepatitis Ambassador : In his latest monumental national role, Okyeame Kwame was officially designated by the Ghana Health Service to lead the charge against viral hepatitis. This is far from a ceremonial title; it is a continuation of over 18 years of personal dedication, massive free public screenings, and advocacy that he spearheaded long before official state instruments caught up with his vision. The Made in Ghana Ambassador : Appointed by the Ministry of Trade and Industry, Okyeame Kwame took patriotism to the studio and the streets. Through his critically acclaimed Made in Ghana album, his deliberate projection of local fashion, and his relentless advocacy for patronizing local goods and services, he became the face of economic nationalism. Tourism Ambassador : Under the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, he leveraged his global appeal and deep understanding of Ghanaian heritage to market the country’s rich cultural tapestry to the rest of the world, championing arts as a vehicle for national identity. Climate Change & Agricultural Advocates: Beyond culture and health, his footprint stretches into environmental sustainability as a former Climate Change Ambassador, alongside his voluntary patriotic efforts supporting agricultural initiatives like Feed Ghana. Why Okyeame Kwame is a National Asset What transforms a talented artist into a national treasure? For Okyeame Kwame, it boils down to three core pillars: Institution Building Over Personal Glory: Many celebrities lend their faces to brands for quick financial gains. Okyeame Kwame often marries his commercial art with national policy, aligning his private initiatives with state goals—frequently offering his time and platform voluntarily out of pure civic duty. Intellectual and Moral Consistency : Popularly known for his articulate delivery, sharp intellect, and gentlemanly demeanor, Okyeame Kwame provides a blueprint for youth mentorship. Whether he is speaking on dyslexia awareness (drawing from his own childhood experiences) or financial literacy for creatives, he projects a polished, progressive image of the Ghanaian intellect. His willingness to go back to school, during the peak of his career encouraged many creatives to also seek higher education. Co-authoring the book Love Locked Down with his wife Annica Nsiah-Apau created an example and a guide for young families seeking stability in their relationships. Longevity and Relevance : Staying relevant in the entertainment industry for five years is hard; staying culturally and socially vital for almost thirty years is a masterpiece of personal branding. He has smoothly transitioned from a youthful rap icon into an elder statesman of Ghanaian creative arts. A Blueprint for the Future As Ghana continues its march toward achieving major health targets – such as the elimination of viral hepatitis – and bolstering local industries, the value of trusted intermediaries between the state and the masses cannot be overstated. Okyeame Kwame represents the ideal synergy between state vision and citizen execution. He proves that true influence is measured by how many lives you can uplift, how many diseases you can help eradicate, and how deeply you can make your people fall in love with their own identity. From the stages of Kumasi and Accra to the high offices of ministries, Okyeame Kwame is not merely an entertainer. He is a national treasure, a living testament to purposeful patriotism, and a true Ghanaian asset.

items.title: Matlaboul Fawzayni : la « maquette » spirituelle de Touba devenue réalité
items.description: Bien avant l'édification de la ville sainte de Touba, Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba en avait esquissé les contours dans une prière. Ce texte, intitulé Matlaboul Fawzayni (« La quête du bienfait des deux mondes »), est considéré par de nombreux érudits mourides comme la « maquette » spirituelle de la cité religieuse. Selon Serigne Khalil Mbacké, petit-fils de Serigne Saliou Mbacké, ce célèbre xasida, rédigé en 1888, année de la fondation de Touba, traduit la vision du fondateur du mouridisme pour la ville sainte. Dès les premiers vers, Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba implore Dieu en ces termes : « Fais de ma demeure la cité bénie de Touba, le bastion de l'obéissance à Allah et du respect de la tradition de l'Envoyé (PSL) pour toujours, et non le foyer des innovations blâmables. » Composé de plus d'une trentaine de vers, Matlaboul Fawzayni présente Touba comme une cité exclusivement vouée à l'adoration de Dieu, à l'enseignement religieux et à l'élévation spirituelle. Le Cheikh y prie pour qu'elle demeure un refuge pour les croyants, un havre de paix pour ceux qui se confient à Allah et un lieu privilégié pour les chercheurs de l'Absolu. Plus d'un siècle après cette invocation, Serigne Khalil Mbacké estime que cette prière s'est largement réalisée. La Grande Mosquée, les daara, notamment Daaray Kamil, les nombreuses écoles coraniques et l'organisation de la vie autour des valeurs religieuses témoignent, selon lui, de l'accomplissement de cette vision. Aujourd'hui, Touba est devenue la deuxième ville la plus peuplée du Sénégal. Chaque année, à l'occasion du Grand Magal, elle accueille plus de deux millions de pèlerins venus du Sénégal et de la diaspora, illustrant le rayonnement spirituel et l'attractivité de cette cité dont les fondements avaient été, dès l'origine, posés dans une fervente prière. Salla GUEYE

items.title: Trump says he will hold off on fresh Iran attack in hope of quick deal
items.description: President Donald Trump has said the U.S. will hold off on a fresh attack on Iran as long as a ​deal can be reached quickly to halt Iran’s nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social ‌platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the vital strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat” He did not name the countries in the post, which followed a call with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, a U.S. ally. “Based on this request, I have agreed, ​for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able ​to rapidly make a DEAL,” Trump wrote. Israel “joins me in this commitment”, he said. IRAN SAYS IT IS BOOSTING DETERRENCE Trump’s apparent de-escalation after ⁠days of threats of new attacks from each side was the latest twist in the war the U.S. and Israel launched five months ago. Attacks have spread ​across the Gulf to the Red Sea and even a Mediterranean facility in Egypt. Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for 20% of the world’s oil and LNG ​before the war, causing energy prices to rise and stoking broader inflation. Eli Cohen, Israel’s energy minister and a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s security cabinet, said there was close security and intelligence coordination between Israel and the U.S. on everything happening in the region. But he added: “With or without an agreement, and regardless of any external commitments, if Iran attempts to renew ​its nuclear programme or advance its ballistic missile industries, we will be there. We will take action, and we will strike.” Trump and Netanyahu met on Tuesday in ​Washington, with an Israeli official saying they had explored all possible paths to curb Iran’s nuclear programme, including diplomacy, economic pressure and force. Tehran denies seeking a nuclear weapon. Iran’s acting defence ‌minister, Brigadier ⁠General Majid Ebn Al-Reza, said Tehran viewed recent U.S. threats as “psychological and cognitive warfare” but was treating them seriously, adding that Iran would boost preparedness and deterrence rather than be caught off guard or remain passive, Press TV reported. In his call with Trump, the Saudi crown prince stressed the “necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions” in the Middle East, according to Saudi Arabia’s state news agency. A White House official told Reuters that the two had spoken but did not provide details. OIL PRICE SURGED LAST MONTH At a cabinet ​meeting on Friday, Trump said he believed ​U.S. negotiators, including his son-in-law Jared ⁠Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, could reach a deal with Iran. As an April ceasefire in the war unravelled last month, benchmark Brent crude futures jumped 24%, and analysts polled by Reuters expect prices to rise further this ​year. Trump has argued that his stated goal of keeping Iran from gaining nuclear weapons justifies higher fuel costs in the ​near term, but the ⁠economic pain has put political pressure on him to find a way to end the war. Adding to the energy industry’s concerns, Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen in recent days began threatening the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the other end of the Red Sea from the Suez Canal, another export route for Saudi crude. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said ⁠on Saturday ​it had received reports of two maritime incidents off Oman. In one, an unknown projectile struck a tanker, ​damaging the engine room. In the other, the master of a tanker reported seeing a large splash and an explosion close to the vessel, though no damage was reported.

items.title: Vatican : un administrateur apostolique nommé à Rabat pendant l'enquête visant le cardinal Lopez Romero
items.description: Le Vatican a nommé un administrateur apostolique pour gouverner provisoirement l'archidiocèse de Rabat dans l'attente des conclusions de son enquête visant l'archevêque de Rabat, le cardinal Cristobal Lopez Romero, qui s'est mis en retrait après des accusations de violences sexuelles révélées par l'AFP. Selon un communiqué du prélat espagnol de 74 ans consulté dimanche par l'agence, le dicastère pour l'Evangélisation des peuples, un ministère du Vatican, a nommé le père Mario Leon Dorado, actuel préfet apostolique de Laâyoune-Sahara, administrateur apostolique « sede plena » de l'archidiocèse de Rabat, avec « tous les droits et facultés accordés aux évêques résidents ». Un administrateur apostolique « sede plena » est un évêque ou un prêtre chargé de gouverner provisoirement un diocèse dont l'évêque titulaire demeure en fonction mais est « empêché ou suspendu », selon le communiqué daté de samedi, adressé aux « frères et soeurs de l'archidiocèse ». « Cette décision intervient dans l'attente des résultats de l'enquête menée par le Saint-Siège me concernant et concernant le diocèse », ajoute le document dans lequel Monseigneur Romero dit continuer durant cette période à être l'évêque titulaire de Rabat, « mais avec la juridiction suspendue ». Le 8 juillet, l'AFP avait révélé qu'au moins cinq femmes accusaient Cristobal Lopez Romero, qui figurait parmi les cardinaux en vue pour succéder en 2025 au pape François (2013-2025), de violences sexuelles et de comportements inappropriés. Aucune plainte n'a, à ce stade, été déposée devant la justice marocaine, ont récemment indiqué le parquet et la police à l'AFP. En réponse à nos sollicitations, le père Cristobal avait déclaré n'avoir « commis ni agression ni violence ni harcèlement sexuel », tout en annonçant se mettre en retrait dans le cadre d'une enquête préliminaire du Vatican. Mgr Mario Leon Dorado, prêtre espagnol membre la congrégation des Oblats de Marie-Immaculée (OMI), exerce son ministère au Sahara marocain depuis près de 25 ans, selon le communiqué. A ce jour, les deux victimes présumées dont l'AFP a recueilli les témoignages n'ont reçu aucune demande d'audition du Saint-Siège, selon une source proche du dossier. Plusieurs sources à l'origine des révélations sur la situation au sein du diocèse de Rabat et réunies au sein du collectif récemment créé « Zéro Tolérance », affirment avoir fait l'objet de mesures de mise à l'écart depuis la publication de l'affaire. Elles ont indiqué dimanche espérer que cette nomination permettra enfin une meilleure prise en compte des victimes et des lanceurs d'alerte par le diocèse.
